#10064. Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session

A mountain of CVEs, a certificate cleanup, and yet more work for Microsoft's patching teams

Microsoft has unleashed a whopper of an update for Azure Linux, packing more than 470 CVE fixes into a single release as the software industry's ever-growing pile of vulnerabilities shows little sign of shrinking.

Over the weekend, Microsoft rolled out Azure Linux 3.0.2022 with fixes covering everything from the Linux kernel to open source packages and container software. The changelog runs to hundreds of entries, so anyone planning to read the whole thing might want to put the kettle on.

Microsoft's release notes contain more than 470 CVE references, although some vulnerabilities appear multiple times because they affect different packages. So that's not necessarily 470 separate security holes, but it's still an impressive amount of patching for one release.

The fixes span OpenSSL, curl, Kubernetes, Docker, QEMU, and a lengthy list of other packages that underpin modern Linux environments. The generic Linux kernel has been updated to version 6.6.161.1.

There's also been some housekeeping following the eMudhra certificate incident, tracked as CVE-2026-114406. Microsoft has removed or distrusted root certificates that could validate compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates, while adding checks in Python and Go to reject the affected certificates. It has also preserved SSL.com TLS trust where required, presumably to avoid fixing one certificate headache by creating another.

Container infrastructure gets plenty of attention, too, with fixes spanning KubeVirt, containerd, Docker Compose, and other components used to keep cloud workloads running. Several CVEs crop up repeatedly across these packages, helping explain the eye-watering number of entries in the changelog.

The release includes less security-focused changes too, including new Dockerfiles, an OpenVMM patch for confidential computing support, fixes for systemd hangs, and adjustments to GRUB Secure Boot metadata.

The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload. As The Register reported earlier today, Linux creator Linus Torvalds reckons there may finally be signs that the flood is easing, at least in some corners of the kernel.

Torvalds said fixes are now arriving faster than new bug reports in the kernel's eBPF subsystem, although he noted that most other areas haven't reached that point. Whether the wider software industry is anywhere close to catching up is another matter, and Microsoft hasn't said if AI-assisted research contributed to the vulnerabilities addressed in this release.

Azure Linux, formerly known as CBL-Mariner, is Microsoft's own Linux distribution, developed primarily for its cloud infrastructure and services. That makes keeping its many components patched rather more important than the modest version-number bump might suggest.

And judging by the size of this latest changelog, Microsoft's patching teams aren't likely to be putting their feet up anytime soon. ®

#10063. Shipping huggingface_hub every week with AI, open tools, and a human in the loop

huggingface_hub is the Python client at the base of the Hugging Face ecosystem. transformers, datasets, diffusers, sentence-transformers and dozens of other libraries depend on it to talk to the Hub. Every week we don't ship a new release is a week of fixes and features stuck on main.

For a long time we released every 4 to 6 weeks. We now release every week from a single GitHub Actions workflow. We built it using open-source tools and open-weights models and kept a human in the loop at the one place where judgment matters. Nothing in this post requires a vendor contract, a closed model, or infrastructure you can't run yourself. That was a design goal from the start since we wanted a workflow other maintainers could pick up and adapt.

By the end of this post, you'll have everything you need to build your own.

The old process was partly automated, mostly manual.

Writing good notes for a new version was the heavy part, aggregating tens of PRs on different topics. Nothing technically hard but a few hours of focused attention. Add the announcements on top and a minor release was easily a half-day of work spread over several days.

So we decided to streamline the whole thing. Looking at that list, the work splits in two.

Some steps are purely mechanical and can be automated: bumping the version, committing, tagging, pushing, opening downstream test branches, opening the post-release PR. Nobody needs to think about those. They just have to happen in the right order, every time, which is what a CI workflow is good at.

The rest is different. Writing release notes, deciding what to highlight, phrasing an announcement for a human audience: that's brain work. It's the kind of judgment that kept the release manual for years. This is where AI comes in, turning a blank page into a solid first draft in seconds. It's also where we have to be careful because a draft that looks confident and is subtly wrong is worse than no draft at all.

When we decided to fix this, we set one constraint up front: every moving part had to be something any maintainer could run themselves. No closed model behind an API we couldn't swap, no proprietary release platform, no secret sauce.

The second principle: the model drafts, a human decides. Language models are good at turning thirty terse PR titles into readable release notes. They are not good at being trusted blindly. So the workflow is human-supervised: the model does the first pass, a deterministic script checks its work, and a human reviews and edits before anything ships (more on that below).

The full workflow is a single file, .github/workflows/release.yml, triggered by hand from the Actions UI. It takes exactly one input:

From there, the jobs run roughly in this order:

The remaining manual steps are reviewing and publishing the draft release notes, and reviewing and posting an internal Slack message. Those two steps are where we want a human in the loop.

Here's the failure mode everyone worries about with AI-generated release notes: the model quietly drops a PR or invents one that isn't in this release. A changelog that's almost right is worse than no changelog because nobody re-checks it.

We don't trust the generated release notes to be complete on the first try, we verify it deterministically. Before the model runs, a Python script retrieves all PRs that belong to the release and stores them as ground truth.

Then model drafts the notes from them. Once done, we check its output against the initial list of PRs:

If anything is missing or extra, we don't fail and we don't ship a wrong file. We hand the discrepancy back to the agent and ask it to fix exactly those PRs:

This is the pattern that makes the whole thing trustworthy: a non-deterministic model wrapped in deterministic guardrails. The model is great at writing prose and unreliable at being exhaustive. So we let it write and let code enforce the consistency.

Completeness is one half. Accuracy is the other. A model summarizing a PR from its title alone will cheerfully invent a code example that doesn't match the real API.

To prevent that, when we fetch PR metadata we also pull the actual documentation diffs from each PR: the unified diff of any .md file under docs/ that the PR touched.

That diff goes into the model's context so when it writes "here's the new CLI command," it's quoting the example the PR author actually wrote in the docs. That's the same logic as before: give the model real source material and a narrow job.

The prompts themselves live as Skills: small Markdown files (SKILL.md plus reference templates) checked into the repo. The release-notes skill spells out how to pick highlights, how to structure sections, when to add a doc link, etc. It reads like onboarding instructions, which is exactly the right mental model.

After the RC is published, the draft GitHub release sits there with the AI's first pass in it. This is where the human comes in:

The reviewer's time goes into polishing, turning a half-day of writing into a fifteen-minute editing session.

We also keep a paper trail to improve over time. We archive two files side by side to a Hugging Face Bucket: the raw AI draft, uploaded at RC time before anyone touches it, and the human-edited version, uploaded when the final release is cut.

Collecting both every week gives us a growing dataset of "what the model wrote" versus "what we wished it wrote". Dataset that we can then reuse to update the agent's skill.

Revamping the release process was a good opportunity to tighten security, especially against supply-chain attacks.

No PyPI token. Publishing uses Trusted Publishing: PyPI verifies a short-lived OIDC token minted by GitHub for this exact workflow, and issues PEP 740 attestations / Sigstore provenance for every artifact. There's no long-lived secret to leak or rotate.

The agent runtime is pinned and verified. We don't curl | bash the latest OpenCode and hope. We pin a version and check its SHA256 before running it:

Open tooling doesn't mean careless tooling.

Almost nothing. A full release (notes plus the Slack announcement, across 20-40 PRs and a few rounds of prompting) costs about $0.25 on Inference Providers. With open weights billed pay-as-you-go, the only real question each week is "is there something worth shipping?", and there always is.

The cadence went from one release every 4 to 6 weeks to once a week. The secondary effects were the interesting ones:

This is the part we cared about most. The workflow is shaped around huggingface_hub but the structure is generic.

To adapt it: fork the workflow file and scripts, point it at your package, rewrite the skill Markdown for your project's voice, set two repo variables (the model ID and your OpenCode version), set up Trusted Publishing on PyPI, and delete the downstream-testing job if you don't have downstreams. The trust-but-verify loop is the part worth reusing as-is. It's what makes a generated artifact safe to ship.

The parts of a release that used to need a half-day of focused human work (writing notes, drafting announcements, coordinating downstream checks) are the parts a model is good at drafting. Everything else is mechanical and fits in a YAML file. The trick was never just "let the AI do it". It's to let the model draft, let deterministic code verify, and let a human decide. It's built entirely from open tools and open weights so the cost rounds to zero and anyone can run it.

The full workflow file is public. If you maintain a Python library, fork it, adapt it, and let us know how it goes!

Thanks for the post! This will help so many people 🤗

#10062. NASA keeps its PROMISE to raid Mars testbeds for parts

Cut-and-shut trundlebot with spiffy new paint job meant to be headed to the Moon in 2028

NASA is moving ahead with its plan to repurpose a Mars rover engineering model as a lunar trundlebot for less than $400 million.

The robot, dubbed PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration), is a cut-and-shut of engineering test articles used for the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers, currently rolling around the Red Planet.

During a weekend briefing, NASA outlined the plan for PROMISE: to land the robot on the lunar surface by late 2028 for an 18-month mission. PROMISE will be preceded by NASA's VIPER trundlebot, which is expected to survive only 100 days on the Moon's surface. PROMISE will carry copies of VIPER's science instruments, including a drill capable of boring 1 meter into the lunar regolith.

Power will come from a Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (RTG) left over from the Cassini mission. NASA acknowledged the fuel was processed some time ago – the Cassini mission to Saturn was launched in 1997 – but anticipates there will be plenty of heat and power for PROMISE's components.

Blue Origin is to deposit the rover on the Moon. NASA awarded the company a $94 million base contract, "with an option period worth an additional $140 million based on performance to deliver PROMISE to the lunar South Pole."

The figures make it difficult to ascertain the exact cost of the PROMISE mission. However, during the briefing, NASA said it had "a pretty firm agreement with JPL to basically deliver the rover to the surface under $400 million." The $400 million includes the lander, which will be Blue Origin's Mark 1.

Earlier this year, The Planetary Society's chief of space policy, Casey Drier, estimated that the mission (including repurposing the hardware developed for Mars and landing it on the Moon) would cost at least $723 million. At the time, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said: "if PROMISE costs even 20 percent of your low-end estimate, we simply will not fly it."

Assuming Isaacman was only talking about the rover, Drier's figure drops to $489 million without launch and landing costs. 20 percent of that is… not going to be enough.

That also doesn't account for the impact of taking away the hardware built for the Mars program. During the briefing, NASA said it was "pretty comfortable" with how the Mars rovers were going and so was happy about repurposing the hardware or, as one speaker put it, "can we give it a new paint job?"

A source told The Register that morale at the agency's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) was not high at present. Raiding successful programs to fulfill the administration's whims is unlikely to have improved the mood of engineers.

Still. Another trundlebot on the Moon. Far better than using that spare RTG for yet another deep space mission, right? ®

#10060. Introducing the FFASR Leaderboard: Benchmarking ASR in the Real World

🚀 First open far-field ASR benchmark: community-driven evaluation across 14 simulated rooms, validated against real-world measurements: https://huggingface.co/spaces/treble-technologies/ffasr

📉 The gap is real and it is large: across all submitted models, far-field WER at low SNR is consistently several times higher than near-field WER on the same speech content

🔬 Methodology you can trust: hybrid wave-based simulation, sim-to-real validation, moving-source splits in beta, held-out audio, and standardized evaluation hardware across all submissions

⚡ Accuracy and speed together: the Pareto front plots average WER against RTFx so you can evaluate the tradeoff that is right for your deployment

👀 More is coming: multi-talker scenarios, microphone array support, and echo cancellation are on the roadmap

The gap between benchmark performance and real-world deployment is one of the more persistent frustrations in ASR development. Models that score well on standard evaluations often behave differently once real room acoustics are involved: reverberation, background noise, microphone distance. The complex interactions between these factors affect performance in ways that clean-speech benchmarks do not capture. The FFASR Leaderboard is our attempt to quantify that gap.

Treble Technologies and Hugging Face are launching the Far-Field ASR (FFASR) Leaderboard, the first open, community-driven benchmark designed to evaluate ASR models under realistic far-field acoustic conditions. It is live now, and we are inviting the community to submit models, explore the results, and help shape what comes next.

Voice interfaces have expanded well beyond the headset and the smartphone. AI voice agents, conference room transcription, in-car assistants, humanoid robots, smart glasses, and hands-free tools are all seeing rapid adoption. What they have in common is that they operate in acoustically complex environments: reverberation, background noise, overlapping sounds, and a microphone that may be anywhere from one to several meters from the speaker.

The dominant ASR evaluation paradigm has not caught up with this reality. Clean, close-microphone benchmarks remain the standard, and while they are useful for measuring core recognition quality, they do not predict far-field performance. A model that performs well on LibriSpeech or other near-field sets may degrade substantially once real room acoustics enter the picture. While there have been several research efforts around far-field and noisy speech evaluation — including CHiME, URGENT, and NOIZEUS — the community has not had a standardized, open way to measure that degradation consistently across models in a continuously updated leaderboard format. That is what FFASR is built for.

A major challenge of far-field evaluation is the availability of data. Collecting far-field recordings across a representative range of room types, microphone distances, and noise conditions at scale is prohibitively expensive with physical measurements alone. Simulation makes it possible to cover that space systematically and to extend coverage over time without a corresponding increase in measurement cost.

Another goal of FFASR is to encourage the development of models that are explicitly robust to these conditions. Leaderboards have historically been effective at directing research effort. By making far-field performance visible and comparable, we hope to raise the priority of real-world acoustic robustness across the field.

The FFASR Leaderboard evaluates models across nine conditions. The four that determine the primary ranking score are (as of 22 June 2026):

To give a sense of what these conditions actually sound like, the samples below let you hear the same speech utterance as dry anechoic audio, then convolved with a room impulse response, and finally with noise added at each SNR tier. The difference between the dry recording and the low-SNR far-field condition is a reasonable proxy for the scale of the problem the leaderboard is measuring.

Two additional columns, Lab Measured and Lab Simulated, serve as a sim-to-real validation track. The leaderboard also includes moving-source splits, currently in beta, which evaluate models against audio where the speaker is in motion rather than stationary. This condition reflects use cases such as humanoid robots, in-car speech, and mobile voice assistants where the acoustic geometry between speaker and microphone changes continuously.

The acoustic data is generated with Treble's hybrid simulation engine, which combines a wave-based solver at low to mid frequencies with geometrical-acoustics modeling at higher frequencies. This approach captures physical phenomena that simpler simulation methods often miss: diffraction, scattering, interference, and modal behavior. The result is simulated data that closely matches measured acoustic conditions, which the Lab Measured and Lab Simulated columns confirm directly by running the same evaluation on both.

Fourteen fully furnished rooms are included in the benchmark, ranging from 20 to 470 m³ and covering bathrooms, living rooms with hallways, offices, classrooms, and restaurant spaces. Each acoustic scene contains one target speaker, recorded in an anechoic chamber to avoid reverberation artifacts from the recording environment, and up to three noise sources. Every scene includes both a transient noise source such as coughing and a continuous noise source such as HVAC, at three SNR levels. This coverage is designed to reflect the actual variety of spaces where deployed voice systems operate.

Alongside WER, the leaderboard reports RTFx (audio seconds per inference second) for every submission, evaluated on an NVIDIA L4 GPU under identical conditions. Accuracy and latency together are what matter in real deployments, and the Pareto front view in the Analysis tab makes that tradeoff explicit.

This benchmark is build on simulated acoustic spaces via Treble Technologies proprietaty simulation engine. An example of the output from the enginge can be found in the Treble10 dataset released last year, which established the simulation pipeline and made far-field RIRs available for training and research. FFASR extends that foundation into a standardized evaluation framework with a held-out test set, consistent normalization, and automated scoring.

With the leaderboard live, a consistent pattern is emerging across all submitted models: the gap between near-field and far-field performance is large, and it grows significantly as SNR decreases. Near-field WER values, on clean dry speech, look comparable to what the same models achieve on established benchmarks. Far-field WER at low SNR tells a different story, often several times higher. The benchmark makes this degradation visible and comparable in a way that was previously difficult to do outside proprietary evaluation pipelines.

The Pareto front of average WER against RTFx is also revealing. There is a genuine spectrum of approaches represented in the current submissions: models that prioritize speed at the cost of some accuracy, models that push accuracy at the cost of throughput, and a smaller number that achieve a competitive position on both axes. Visualizing these tradeoffs against far-field accuracy rather than clean-speech accuracy produces a materially different picture of where the real differences between systems lie. The Analysis tab is worth exploring beyond the main ranking table.

One observation worth highlighting for developers: the leaderboard reports both near-field (dry) and far-field WER side by side. This separation is intentional and useful. It makes it possible to distinguish between a model that is genuinely accurate and one that is accurate but brittle to acoustic conditions, which matters for deciding whether to invest in far-field fine-tuning, speech enhancement preprocessing, or a different architecture altogether.

Open the Submit tab on the FFASR Leaderboard, paste a Hugging Face model ID, and evaluation runs server-side against the held-out dataset. The pipeline supports Whisper variants, IBM Granite Speech, Cohere Transcribe, Wav2Vec2 and HuBERT CTC heads, SpeechBrain ASR, and most other ASR architectures on the Hub without any custom configuration.

For teams using more complex inference stacks, including systems that combine speech enhancement with ASR, a custom evaluator option allows you to define your own evaluate() function. Custom evaluators run on Hub Jobs after moderator review, and the submission notes field is a good place to document any preprocessing steps so results are interpretable by others.

The held-out evaluation set uses 2,000 anechoic speech samples across 14 rooms at three SNR tiers, approximately 8 hours of audio per condition, with Whisper-style text normalization applied consistently. The audio is not exposed to submitters, to avoid test-set contamination.

The conditions we are actively exploring for future tracks include multi-talker scenarios, where more than one speaker is active simultaneously, microphone array evaluation, covering beamforming and spatial filtering approaches, and echo cancellation, relevant for any device that plays audio while also listening.

What we build next will depend on where the community tells us the gaps are largest. If you work on a deployment environment or a use case that is not well represented in the current benchmark, we want to hear from you. The FFASR Leaderboard is designed to grow, and the direction it grows should reflect real needs.

Submit your model, explore the Analysis tab, post your ideas and suggestions on the FFASR forum, and help us build a benchmark that is actually useful for the problems the field is working on.

Far-Field ASR — clean / noisy / reverberant benchmark

Btw one related idea I've had sitting on the back of my mind: there's a class of synthetic audio scenarios that don't really occur naturally but are both tricky and relevant to real deployments.

Most ASR models lately seem geared toward clean meeting transcription. But if you run a Granola style setup that pulls every audio stream on your machine and mixes them together, things get messy fast. The system audio from the meeting, your physical hardware mic, and sometimes your own voice echoing back through the meeting can all be mixed/delayed/noisy in the same track the model sees. (I use VibeVoice for this myself since I figured it would be more robust; it's held up okay, but I haven't done a real comparison)

Mixed multi-stream audio like that feels like a natural fit for the kind of robustness/"real world scenario" this benchmark is measuring, even though it's a synthetic condition rather than a recorded room

#10059. AWS Weekly Roundup: Amazon Polly Generative engine, TorchNeuron for Trainium, and more (October 26, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The Amazon Polly Generative engine upgrade added 14 new voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice.

Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo.

The rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the issue rather than a severity label. It ranks issues by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation currently requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future.

The “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the AWS WAF mitigations for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon).

Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer.

The numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches that caught my attention this week.

Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine – The Generative engine now runs a larger, more expressive catalog: 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales, with 14 new voices across 9 locales and Hindi and Finnish generally available for the first time. Two of the new voices are Brazilian Portuguese, Leo and Carolina. It is a drop-in upgrade, so the voice names, the same SynthesizeSpeech call, and the price all stay the same while the output gets more natural.

AWS announces TorchNeuron: native PyTorch support for AWS Trainium (public beta) – TorchNeuron is an open source PyTorch backend that lets you run your model on Trainium by switching to .to(‘neuron’), a configuration change instead of a rewrite, with eager execution and torch.compile intact. It integrates with the Neuron Kernel Interface for custom operators, and it works on Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. If you want the bigger picture on why hardware choice should not lock in your software, the AWS Insights piece on that theme is a good companion read, and the release lands alongside AWS Neuron 2.33.

New ways to customize models with Amazon SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs – Training sessions are now generally available, giving you control of the post-training loop, including custom loss functions and reward signals, while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage. You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes, and the meter stops while your reward function scores a batch. There is a full technical walkthrough, the training session APIs, and new support for Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8, and Ministral 3.

Structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock – You can now get schema-compliant JSON back from any Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock, across both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. That makes jobs like pulling every required field from a financial report, parsing clinical notes, or routing support tickets by intent far more reliable to automate.

Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime – You can migrate self-managed Valkey or Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 into ElastiCache Serverless with zero downtime, meaning zero errors returned to the client during the move, measured the way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, then choose a manual or automatic cutover, with no third-party replication tools. It is available in all commercial Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Other AWS news Here are some additional projects and posts that you might find interesting.

Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry – AWS Agent Registry is a managed catalog for MCP servers, agents, and agent skills, so an orchestrator can search approved capabilities at runtime instead of compiling every tool in at build time. This walkthrough shows the discover, instantiate, and execute loop in a working sample, with search results that return connection metadata but never invocation credentials.

Tokenomics for coding agents: benchmark cost and quality on your own code – Coding assistants replay a growing transcript on every turn, so their cost math is nothing like ordinary inference. This post gives you open source tooling to measure model, harness, and hosting choices on your own repositories and build a cost-and-quality frontier you own, with sample results where routing came out 44.7 percent cheaper for 4.8 percent lower mean quality.

How U.S. Bank migrated 119 TB from Oracle Exadata to Amazon RDS for Oracle – U.S. Bank moved four Oracle Exadata databases totaling about 119 TB to Amazon RDS for Oracle using a config-driven pipeline built on Oracle XTTS, AWS DataSync, and Amazon EFS. The initial baseline copy finished in about 7 days with zero data loss and cutovers averaging roughly four hours per database, over a bandwidth-capped Direct Connect link.

Upcoming AWS events Mark your calendars for these upcoming events.

AWS re:Invent – AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas, with more than 2,200 sessions. The session catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so now is the time to build your schedule.

AWS Community Days – AWS Community Day Brasil Norte takes place in Belém on October 31, closing out the 2026 Brazilian community season. Check the hub for events near you.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

For a small model (think handwriting recognition, say, 6x8 pixels), it is actually possible to construct a formal proof that the model will correctly identify digits and characters correctly. However, it is usually more expedient just to test with a large sample of typical inputs. In such cases, an error ratio smaller than what a human would produce, and the low risk of failure makes this approach acceptable. However, for LLMs and models of the size typically used in self driving, it is practically impossible to verify the model (think heat death of the universe) using formal methods. The best that one can do is identify the desired outcome and perform statistical tests to determine the error percentage. When it comes to applications such as criminal sentencing, self driving, and applicant selection where mistakes expose the model user to substantial liability, AI may be more appropriate in an assistive role where a human must be in the decision loop. Even so, there are yet a large number of AI applications where mediocre performance (i.e. good enough, with occasional errors) is in fact good enough to justify the cost savings. It is programs like the one proposed here which represent a structural danger to society: because of doctrines like sovereign immunity, a state which certifies a model as "safe" does not actually have any responsibility for the harm caused by such a representation. That is, a company which relies on the state's safety certification can avoid liability for harm caused by the model, and the state has neither the responsibility nor the incentive to test the model in an intellectually honest and formally rigorous way. Thus, the cost of testing the model is borne by the state, the liability for mistakes is borne by the public at large, and the disproportionate profit such an arrangement facilitates accrues to the benefit of private corporations. Thus, the cost of testing the model is borne by the state, the liability for mistakes is borne by the public at large, and the disproportionate profit such an arrangement facilitates accrues to the benefit of private corporations.

#10057. Microsoft takes three decades to make Sticky Keys less sticky

Windows preview adds a 'don't ask again' option to accessibility prompts, sparing users a trip through Settings

Windows testers are getting a new option in the Sticky Keys and Filter Keys dialogs – one to banish the pop-ups without needing to venture deep into Settings.

It's only taken several decades for Microsoft to put the off switch where the interruption actually happens. The accessibility features themselves are useful, though triggering their activation prompts by accident is another matter.

Once enabled, Sticky Keys let users press modifier keys (such as Control) one at a time instead of holding them down together. For example, rather than holding Control and pressing C to copy, a user can press and release Control, then press C. Filter Keys, meanwhile, ignores brief or repeated keystrokes and adjusts the keyboard's repeat behavior.

However, the dialogs are of little use to people who don't need the features, and they can pop up at the most inconvenient moments. Tap Shift five times, and you'll see what we mean: Windows chimes and shows a dialog asking whether you'd like to turn on Sticky Keys. Dismiss it, hit Shift five times, and there it is again.

Or hold down the right Shift key for eight seconds to be treated to the Filter Keys pop-up.

You can stop this behavior elsewhere in the system, but it requires a trek through Windows settings. The change, introduced in the Experimental Windows Insider Build 26340.9882, adds an option to the Sticky Keys or Filter Keys dialogs to dismiss the prompts permanently.

It's a small change, but one that should spare users an irritating interruption. Better late than never – even if "never ask me again" has taken roughly three decades to reach the dialog.

Former Microsoft engineer Charles Opperman said he wrote the dialog in early 1995 "after @bradsilverberg kids kept activating StickeyKeys [sic] while playing Space Cadet pinball."

Opperman added that a link to Settings was added in Windows 98 or what would become Windows 2000, and a checkbox was considered even then, but it wasn't deemed a priority. Users could turn off the prompt via settings. Now the option is front and center.

The option is also rolling out in the Windows Insider Beta channel, although Microsoft has not announced a general release date. ®

#10056. Accelerating Transformers Fine-Tuning with NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel

HuggingFace Transformers has become the foundation of the open-source AI ecosystem, and the recent Transformers v5 release strengthened it with first-class support for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, now the dominant architecture for frontier models. v5 ships the MoE foundations: expert backends, dynamic weight loading, and distributed execution that make MoE extensible and easy to build on.

NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel is an open library part of the NVIDIA NeMo framework for building custom generative AI models at scale. NeMo AutoModel builds cleanly on top of v5, adding Expert Parallelism, DeepEP fused all-to-all dispatch, and TransformerEngine kernels, and it leans on v5's dynamic weight loading to bring those optimizations to a broad and growing set of model families. The payoff is 3.4-3.7x higher training throughput and 29-32% less GPU memory on fine-tuning MoE models than native Transformers v5, using the same from_pretrained() API: a single import line, with no other code changes.

This blog details how this combination works and how users can fine-tune MoE models faster without changing their APIs.

The rise of MoE models has introduced new challenges to efficient training: Routing tokens across hundreds of experts, fusing expert matmuls into a single kernel, sharding weights across GPUs, and overlapping communication with computation all require infrastructure beyond what a general-purpose library provides out of the box.

Transformers v5 (“v5”) introduced first-class MoE support such as expert backends, dynamic weight loading, and tensor parallel plans for distributed execution. In addition, v5 made distributed training first-class by integrating PyTorch's DeviceMesh directly into from_pretrained().

NeMo AutoModel builds on top of v5 by subclassing AutoModelForCausalLM, and adding Expert Parallelism (EP), DeepEP fused all-to-all dispatch, and TransformerEngine kernels. DeepEP is the piece v5 doesn't have yet: it overlaps communication with expert compute. And because NeMo AutoModel rides v5's reversible weight conversion to load each model, it can focus its engineering on these reusable core ops instead of per-model checkpoint plumbing, while save_pretrained() still emits standard HF checkpoints that tools like vLLM and SGLang can load.

The next section walks through how the two work together and the performance gains we measured, from full fine-tuning NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B across 16 nodes down to single-node models such as Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B.

One of NeMo AutoModel's goals is API compatibility with HuggingFace Transformers to enable open-source community. NeMoAutoModelForCausalLM subclasses AutoModelForCausalLM, so any code that works with HF models works with AutoModel too.

Here's what loading a model looks like in both. Only the import changes:

That single import does a lot of work. For popular MoE architectures like Qwen3, NVIDIA Nemotron, GPT-OSS, and DeepSeek V3, NeMo AutoModel ships hand-tuned implementations with TransformerEngine attention, fused linear layers, and custom expert kernels. For everything else, it falls back to vanilla HF while still applying optimizations like Liger kernel patching, among others. And whichever path it takes, the resulting model is ready to scale: pass a device_mesh and you have multi-GPU training without further rewrites.

Where NeMo AutoModel really shines is scaling MoE models to multi-GPU training. To train Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B with Expert Parallelism across 8 GPUs, one adds the distributed mesh configuration:

This gives speed, scalability and memory-optimizations with FSDP2, Expert Parallelism, TransformerEngine kernels and DeepEP dispatch, all from a from_pretrained() call.

We evaluated NeMo AutoModel in two regimes: full fine-tuning a frontier-scale 550B model across 16 nodes, and training two 30B MoE models on a single node. The 550B result shows why Expert Parallelism is essential at scale; the 30B results quantify the per-GPU speedup over Transformers v5.

Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B is a 550B-parameter hybrid model shipping with Mamba2, LatentMoE, and Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). We benchmark a full fine-tune: every parameter is updated and the Adam optimizer state is materialized, which at this scale spans 16 H100 nodes (128 GPUs).

Why there is no Transformers v5 column. Transformers v5 runs out of memory at this scale, so there is no v5 number to report here. AutoModel's Expert Parallelism shards the experts across GPUs to bring the footprint within budget, which is what lets the full fine-tune run. The 30B comparisons below show the same advantage where v5 fits.

We benchmarked three approaches on a single node with 8x H100 80GB GPUs: HF Transformers v4 (hub code), HF Transformers v5 (with best available optimizations), and NeMo AutoModel (EP=8 + custom kernels).

A note on the routing gate. The NeMo AutoModel numbers below use a balanced routing gate, which forces tokens to be distributed uniformly across experts. This emulates the ideal operating point an MoE is trained toward: a well-trained model's load-balancing loss drives expert utilization to near-uniform, so balanced routing reflects the steady-state a real workload converges to (and removes the straggler noise that random dummy tokens otherwise inject into expert parallelism). v4/v5 run their native router on the same dummy tokens. The balanced gate therefore measures NeMo AutoModel at its target MoE operating point, and the v4/v5 columns reflect their out-of-the-box behavior.

Why v4 deadlocks: Transformers v4 stores Qwen3 MoE experts as a ModuleList of 128 individual MLP modules, each separately FSDP-wrapped. The forward pass uses a data-dependent loop that only iterates experts that received tokens. With different data per rank, different ranks skip different experts, causing mismatched FSDP AllGather/ReduceScatter collectives and an indefinite hang. Transformers v5 fixes this by storing experts as fused 3D parameter tensors (no per-expert modules, no per-expert FSDP collectives).

v4 config: trust_remote_code=True (NVIDIA's hub modeling code). The hub code's expert loop is FSDP-safe (iterates all experts regardless of token assignment), so it doesn't deadlock like Qwen3 v4.

The 3.4-3.7x speedup from NeMo AutoModel over Transformers v5 comes from three sources:

Expert Parallelism reduces memory pressure. EP=8 distributes expert weights across GPUs, cutting the per-GPU MoE footprint by 8x. For Qwen3, this drops peak memory from 68.2 GiB to 48.1 GiB (-29%). For Nemotron Nano, it drops from 62.1 GiB to 42.5 GiB (-32%), freeing headroom for larger batch sizes or longer sequences.

DeepEP fuses communication with computation. Instead of separate AllGather/ReduceScatter collectives for expert routing, DeepEP fuses token dispatch and combines into optimized GPU kernels, overlapping communication with expert computation.

TransformerEngine kernels accelerate core operations. TE's fused attention, linear layers, and RMSNorm implementations provide consistent speedups over their PyTorch/Flash Attention equivalents across all layer types, not just MoE layers.

One of the most impactful features in Transformers v5 is the experts_implementation parameter, which includes three expert backends:

The grouped_mm backend is the key training optimization: instead of looping over experts one by one, it sorts tokens by their assigned expert and executes a single fused grouped matrix multiplication.

NeMo AutoModel takes this further. For models with custom implementations, it uses DeepEP fused all-to-all dispatch combined with grouped GEMM kernels and TransformerEngine linear layers. The progression looks like:

In NeMo AutoModel, the expert backend is configured through BackendConfig:

Transformers v5 also ships an Expert Parallelism path. It shards expert weights across GPUs. The GroupedGemmParallel style loads only each device's local experts, and RouterParallel routes tokens and combines results with an all_reduce. It's neatly built on v5's existing tensor-parallel machinery. Enabling it makes the model's tp_plan return its expert plan, so expert parallelism shares the device budget with data parallelism (ep × dp = world_size). For the single-node 30B benchmarks here, we found plain data-parallel v5 (dp=8, ep=1) to be the fastest v5 configuration, so that's the v5 setup we report.

NeMo AutoModel takes a complementary approach tuned for multi-GPU MoE training. It makes EP its own parallelism dimension, a dedicated moe_mesh alongside (rather than carved from) the data-parallel mesh, using PyTorch's DTensor with Shard(0). Because the expert mesh is orthogonal to data parallelism, the two compose on the same devices. On 8 GPUs NeMo AutoModel runs ep=8 and dp=8 together, so every GPU trains on its own data shard while holding only 1/8 of the experts. Expert weights are physically sharded across GPUs along the expert dimension.

With ep_size=8 on 8 GPUs, each GPU holds only 1/8 of the expert parameters. For a model like Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B with ~55 GiB of expert weights, EP reduces the per-GPU expert footprint from ~55 GiB to ~6.8 GiB, making training possible where FSDP-only approaches run out of memory.

On top of EP, NeMo AutoModel integrates DeepEP that fuses the token routing into optimized GPU kernels, and delivers significant speedups when combined with grouped GEMM for grouped expert computation. In our large-scale MoE benchmarks, DeepEP + grouped GEMM reduced cost per iteration by 47% on the full DeepSeek V3 671B model compared to all-gather + looped expert baselines.

Transformers v5 also introduced a dynamic weight loading system through WeightConverter and WeightRenaming. This enables MoE checkpoint to be stored in fused 3D tensors for more efficient execution. The WeightConverter applies composable operations to transform checkpoint tensors on-the-fly during from_pretrained().

NeMo AutoModel is a direct consumer of this v5 API. Over 20 model types use this mechanism through MODELS_REQUIRING_TENSOR_MERGING, including Mixtral, Qwen2 MoE, Qwen3 MoE, DeepSeek V2/V3, OLMoE, and more. The conversions are fully reversible: save_pretrained() produces standard HF-format checkpoints that any downstream tool can load.

To try NeMo AutoModel, please visit our official documentation page to get started.

NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel is the natural next step for HuggingFace users scaling up model training. By building directly on Transformers v5, AutoModel provides a zero-friction upgrade path: change one import line and get a model instance that is more than three times as fast.

On Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B, this delivers 3.4-3.7x higher training throughput with 29-32% less GPU memory compared to the best Transformers v5 configuration. And because true Expert Parallelism shards experts across GPUs, the same path scales up to full fine-tuning a 550B model like Nemotron 3 Ultra across 16 nodes, the regime where Expert Parallelism becomes essential to fit the model in memory. Because NeMo AutoModel checkpoints are standard HF-format safetensors, you can deploy them on inference frameworks like vLLM and SGLang.

The code, configs, and benchmark scripts are all available in the NeMo AutoModel repository.

Core contributors to this work, listed alphabetically by last name: Adil Asif, Hemil Desai, Alexandros Koumparoulis, and Huiying Li.

#10055. AWS Weekly Roundup: GPT-6.1 Terra on Bedrock, Step Functions as agent tools, and more (November 2, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

The agentic launches that stayed with me last week had nothing to do with how capable a model is. They were about reach. AWS Step Functions, which already orchestrates over 220 AWS services, can now be handed to an agent as a tool, so workflows teams already trust became callable without a rewrite. In the same week, the AI blog published how one engagement platform exposed roughly 400 internal API operations the same way. Neither story involves rebuilding anything, only describing what exists and letting the agent find it.

The other thread was cost. OpenAI’s newest Terra model reached Amazon Bedrock priced well below the model beside it, and two post-quantum launches landed for a deadline nobody can put on a calendar yet. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesOpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, and what interests me is where it sits rather than what it tops. Terra is the everyday-workload line of the GPT-6 family. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than both. Those are OpenAI’s figures, not an independent test. The price is what I would check first: input and output tokens are at least 50% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It takes up to 1 million input tokens with text and image input, and you can reach it from the Bedrock APIs or ChatGPT Work and Codex.

AWS Step Functions workflows are now available as AI agent tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, which connects agents to tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The division of labor is the idea: the agent decides when to run a workflow and what input to pass; Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. A support agent can trigger a refund, and the eligibility check, the manager approval, and the credit still happen in that order every time, because the ordering was never the model’s to improvise. Your existing Standard and Express workflows qualify as connector targets, and agents can also look up runs. It’s available in all Regions where AgentCore Gateway is, at standard rates.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation – You can now establish a shared secret with a post-quantum algorithm using AWS KMS keys, with private keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs. All three NIST FIPS 203 parameter sets are supported through Encapsulate, which produces a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext, and Decapsulate, which recovers it. The threat is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary records today’s key exchange and recovers the secret once quantum computers are powerful enough. It’s available everywhere KMS runs except the Middle East (UAE and Bahrain) and China Regions. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL added post-quantum TLS key exchange the same week, on versions 18 and higher.

AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation – You can now carry a user’s identity with their request to AWS services in another Region. This removes a genuine architectural constraint: trusted identity propagation used to require every service accessing that identity to sit in the same Region, which left two unappealing options, broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users, or consolidating all your services into a single Region. Now the identity travels with the request automatically, so you grant access by user and group membership and audit who accessed what. It’s available at no additional cost everywhere IAM Identity Center runs.

Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) – You can now run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU, the practical answer to work that only ever uses a fraction of one, like small-model inference and multi-model serving. You declare the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally cap its share of GPU compute, and ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale, with no code changes. It works on ECS Managed Instances and ECS on Amazon EC2, and on Managed Instances it watches the MPS control daemon and replaces the instance if it turns unhealthy. It’s available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances – You can now have AWS Lambda fetch only the files needed at each stage of startup instead of pulling a whole container image first, which AWS puts at up to 70% off container startup time. You create a SOCI index, push it to Amazon ECR, point the image URI at the indexed tag, and Lambda detects it automatically. The technique also reached Amazon SageMaker AI training and processing jobs, with benchmarks: lazy loading held at 3 to 11 seconds regardless of image size, against a median 3 minutes 42 seconds for a 13.2 GB image, a range they report as 8x to 46x.

Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports Kubernetes Gateway API – You can now declare how traffic reaches your applications with Gateway and HTTPRoute resources on Amazon EKS without installing a separate controller, and EKS Auto Mode provisions and manages the underlying AWS load balancing infrastructure. You get HTTP and gRPC routing, cross-namespace routing, weighted traffic splitting, header-based routing, and automatic TLS certificate discovery through AWS Certificate Manager. Existing Ingress workloads keep working alongside them, so this is additive rather than a migration. Gateway API support is included with EKS Auto Mode; standard load balancing charges apply.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

How Nubank automated disaster recovery with the AWS DevOps Agent – Nubank serves more than 140 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, and classifies over 300 business flows as critical, each tested on a regulator’s schedule. Nubank reports that handing evidence collection and report writing to the AWS DevOps Agent cut a test cycle from about 4.3 hours to roughly 40 minutes, and quadrupled flow coverage in 2026 to more than 160. One execution terminated more than 900 EKS instances under synthetic traffic with AWS Fault Injection Service, producing the evidence its regulator needed.

How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway – Roughly 400 internal REST API operations, built by 25 teams, sitting in private VPCs across seven Regions, with tenant identity that could never become a parameter the model gets to set. MoEngage estimates the managed path saved about six months of platform engineering. The detail worth stealing: a full tool listing would have crossed 20,000 tokens per connection, so agents search for tools by describing a task instead of receiving the catalog.

Reducing petabyte-scale S3 storage costs with evidence-based lifecycle rules – The hard part isn’t deciding to act, it’s knowing which data has gone cold and where it can safely live. This uses S3 Storage Lens groups and Storage Class Analysis to prove access patterns before moving anything. In the engagement described, 5.8 PB of logs in Amazon S3 Standard at approximately $241,000 per month showed an access ratio below 0.1% past 90 days, and a 90-day transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval cut the bill by roughly 70%, a figure the author ties to that workload.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, with more than 2,200 sessions. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders. The 2026 season is winding down as re:Invent approaches, so check the hub for what’s still on.

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. #10054. Insight about how 'nature makes no leaps' promises better robot predictions

Machine learning researchers have developed a technique that allows world models to make better predictions about how objects will behave.

World models are used to train physical AI systems like robots how to navigate the real world. They predict the consequences of actions. But they do so based on observed data. These models could provide better direction to robots if they were able to make inferences about possible actions without being trained for all the possible outcomes.

Randall Balestriero (Brown University, AMI Labs), Kerda Varaku, and Turing Award winner Yann LeCun (NYU, AMI Labs) describe an approach that might allow that to happen in a pre-print paper, "Counterfactual World Models: Natura Non Facit Saltus."

The Latin refers to Gottfried Leibniz's axiom "nature makes no leaps," which had a good run until it ran headlong into quantum mechanics. Yet for the authors, the saying explains how they have been able to devise a method for zero-shot physics inference.

Counterfactual world models, said Balestriero in an email to The Register use "the mismatch between your prediction and the real world to figure out what did you get wrong, and from that you can better understand what happened for better future predictions, debugging, reasoning, all at test time."

Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models, developed by LeCun and colleagues back in 2023, have been proposed for robots because they can take an action as input and ask what the world would be like with that action.

But a JEPA world model produces an average of outcomes and would not be able to anticipate counterfactual scenarios – events that didn't happen. The technique that the researchers developed is not specific to JEPAs – it can be applied to any world model that predicts the average next state under any action. But JEPA models are particularly well suited to being adapted.

Balestriero said that the counterfactual world model experiments were done using off-the-shelf encoders (DINOv2 and MAE) without any fine-tuning and only a small predictor trained on top. Creating a counterfactual world model from that starting point would only require minor additions.

Counterfactual world models predict alternative scenarios more effectively by inferring possibilities from what did occur.

"In causal inference, answering 'What would have happened had I acted differently?' takes three steps," explained Balestriero. "You use what you observed to learn something about those hidden factors, you change the action, and you predict again with the hidden factors kept exactly as they were.

"Our counterfactual world model does all three steps with one subtraction."

Balestriero cited an example from the paper: a boat crossing a river with a hidden current and how the JEPA world model and counterfactual world model predicted the boat's movements.

"The world model predicted where the boat would end up after steering left, and it actually ended up two meters further downstream," he explained. "Those two meters are the signature of the current that occurred. To answer 'where would the boat be had I steered right?', we take the world model's prediction for steering right and add the same two meters. In other words, the counterfactual is what actually happened, plus the difference between the model's predictions for the alternative action and for the action taken.

"Physics enters to justify this rule, not as an equation the model fits. Over a short time, the effect of the action and the effect of the current each grow in proportion to the duration, while their interaction grows only with its square, so over short steps they simply add up, like forces.

"We prove that the fraction of the disturbance's effect that this rule gets wrong shrinks with the square of the time step, and that no method using the same ordinary data can do better than this rate in the worst case."

Counterfactual world models have three likely uses, according to Balestriero. The first is having a robot retry an action after a surprise event.

"When an attempt fails because of something the robot could not see, such as an unexpected load, a current or a weak motor, the counterfactual world model lets it estimate which action would have worked in that same situation," he explained. "In our simulated tasks, choosing the action this way reaches the goal in 35 to 69 percent of events, against 14 to 23 percent for a planner that knows the true simulator but ignores the observed outcome. With two more attempts on the same event, success rises to 51 to 97 percent."

He also sees these models being useful for adapting to persistent fault, like a miscalibrated motor, and helping people understand failures.

"World models are trained to predict, and they are getting good at it," said Balestriero. "But a robot, a car or a drone acting in the real world is constantly surprised by things it could not see coming. After a surprise, the useful question is no longer what was expected, but what would have happened had it acted differently in that same situation. You need that answer to debug a failure, to tell a bad decision from bad luck, or to decide what to do on the next attempt, and prediction alone does not provide it."

The researchers initial attempts to address the issue involved adding a learned component to the world model that infers whatever hidden disturbance (e.g. the current in the boat scenario) affected the anticipated outcome. But that approach was too fragile.

"Trying to understand why led to the theory," explained Balestriero. "Learning the disturbance from ordinary data is not just hard, it is impossible in general: the hidden noise can be relabeled differently for each action without changing a single prediction, so the data cannot tell you which labeling is the right one. The missing piece has to come from outside the data. For physical systems, it comes from the fact that forces add and that their interaction builds up slowly in time. Once you accept that, the learned disturbance model becomes unnecessary: the gap between what happened and what was predicted already carries the information you need, and you carry it over to the other action."

Balestriero said that control engineers have been implementing corrections of this sort for decades, to tune hand-built models.

"What was missing was why the same correction is justified for learned world models that see the world through images, what can and cannot be recovered without paired data, and where it breaks," he said. "The paper answers these questions by connecting causal inference, control and world models. The title comes from Leibniz's law of continuity, natura non facit saltus, 'nature makes no leaps,' which is precisely the property that makes all of this work."

The researchers' paper was provided to The Register prior to its release on ArXiv. It is expected to be released this week. ®

#10053. Run a vLLM Server on HF Jobs in One Command

You can spin up a private, OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint on Hugging Face infrastructure with a single command — no servers to provision, no Kubernetes, pay-per-second. Once it's up, you can query it from your laptop, a notebook, or anywhere else.

It's the quickest way to stand up a model for tests, evals, or batch generation. (If you're after a managed, production-ready service instead, that's what Inference Endpoints are for — more on when to pick which at the end.)

hf jobs run is docker run for HF infrastructure. We use the official vllm/vllm-openai image, ask for a GPU with --flavor, and expose vLLM's port with --expose:

--expose 8000 routes the container's port through HF's public jobs proxy (see the Serve Models guide for the full reference). The command prints the URL your server is reachable at:

6a381ca1953ed90bfb947332 is your job ID. Keep track of it, we'll need it. We'll use as a placeholder for it in the rest of the post.

Give it a couple of minutes to download weights and boot. When the logs show Application startup complete, you're live.

vLLM speaks the OpenAI API, and every request just needs your HF token as a bearer token. The quickest way to hit it is curl:

which returns the usual OpenAI-style JSON, with choices[0].message.content holding "Hello! How can I assist you today? 😊".

Or, from Python, point the OpenAI client at the exposed URL and pass the token as the API key:

Quick health check before you start: curl https://--8000.hf.jobs/v1/models -H "Authorization: Bearer $(hf auth token)" should list the model.

🔐 The endpoint is gated, not public. Every request must carry an HF token with read access to the job's namespace. A plain browser visit will be rejected. In effect, the jobs proxy is your API gate: access is scoped to you (and your org). That's fine for private use, but treat the URL accordingly: don't share it expecting it to be open, and don't paste your token into untrusted places. If you need finer-grained or public access, put a proper gateway in front instead. Or see HF Jobs or Inference Endpoints? below.

Jobs are billed per second, so stop the server when you're done:

The --timeout you set is a safety net (it'll auto-stop), but cancelling explicitly is cheaper. An a10g-large runs at $1.50/hour — check hf jobs hardware for the full price list and pick the smallest flavor that fits your model.

The same command scales to much larger models — pick a beefier --flavor and tell vLLM to shard the model across the GPUs with --tensor-parallel-size. For example, the 122B Qwen3.5 mixture-of-experts model on 2× H200:

--tensor-parallel-size should match the number of GPUs in the flavor (h200x2 → 2, h200x8 → 8). Run hf jobs hardware to see what's available and give bigger models a longer --timeout, since they take longer to download and load. For large models, H200 flavors are usually the best value.

The --max-model-len 32768 --max-num-seqs 256 flags are specific to this model: Qwen3.5-122B is a hybrid Mamba/attention architecture with a 256K-token default context, which doesn't leave enough memory for vLLM's default batch settings. Capping the context length and concurrent-sequence count keeps it within the GPUs' memory. If a model fails to start with an out-of-memory or cache-block error, dialing these two down is the first thing to try. Everything else (the exposed URL, the OpenAI client, the token auth) stays exactly the same.

Prefer a chat window over curl? A few lines of Gradio point at the same endpoint. Add --reasoning-parser deepseek_r1 to the vllm serve command so Qwen3's thinking comes back as a separate field (not necessary, but helpful), then run this code locally (you'll just need the job ID):

Run it, open http://127.0.0.1:7860, and chat — reasoning streams into the collapsible panel, the answer below.

Need to debug a startup failure, watch GPU memory, or tail logs interactively? You can open a shell straight into the running job. Launch it with --ssh and make sure your public key is registered at huggingface.co/settings/keys:

You're now inside the container, where you can run nvidia-smi, inspect the process, or poke at the model directly — which makes debugging and monitoring much easier than reading logs from the outside. SSH support requires huggingface_hub >= 1.20.0.

The same endpoint can back a terminal coding agent. Pi is a provider-agnostic agent harness. Point it at the job and you get a Read/Write/Edit/Bash agent running on your own self-hosted model.

One thing to set up first: agents drive the model through tool calls, and vLLM only accepts those if the server is launched with tool calling enabled. So relaunch with --enable-auto-tool-choice and a --tool-call-parser matching the model family (hermes for Qwen3). Agents also benefit from a stronger model, so this is a good place to bring in the bigger one:

Then add the job as a custom provider in ~/.pi/agent/models.json:

The model you spun up a couple of commands ago, now driving an interactive coding agent in your terminal.

HF Jobs isn't the only way to serve a model on Hugging Face. Inference Endpoints are our managed product for the same job, and which one fits depends on what you're after.

Reach for HF Jobs when you want maximum flexibility and control: it's just docker run on HF infrastructure, so you pick the image, the exact vllm serve flags, and the hardware, and you pay per second for as long as the job runs. That makes it a great fit for experiments, one-off evals, batch generation, or kicking the tires on a model before committing to anything.

Reach for Inference Endpoints when you want something more production-ready. They add the operational niceties a long-lived service needs: finer-grained access control (an endpoint can be public, protected, or private), and scale-to-zero, so you're not billed during periods of inactivity. If you're standing up a durable endpoint rather than running a job, that's the tool to grab.

This post sticks to vLLM, but the same expose-a-port pattern works with any OpenAI-compatible server. To serve GGUFs with llama.cpp or run SGLang instead, see the Serve Models on Jobs guide, which walks through those backends.
