#9992. 30 years of Internet transfers with curl

Thirty years ago, on November 11, 1996 the young Brazilian student Rafael Sagula posted the source code for his tiny HTTP download tool online. That was httpget 0.1: a little over 100 lines of C code. Bare bones source code with almost no error checks and limited functionality.

When I found the source code of that initial httpget release just days after Rafael put it online, I had no idea how HTTP worked. The language to speak over the network to ask for resources. Okay, I already knew we call it protocol but not a lot more. I also had never heard of neither httpget nor Rafael before. I imagine that I found httpget by searching on Altavista since this was before Google, but I can’t recall the details.

Seeing the simplicity of this code it was not difficult to immediately spot the fundamental basics of the protocol. I presume maybe in the same vain how countless others in decades to follow also have thought of it when seeing the details for the first time. Much later I would come to understand that to be an illusion of simplicity, but in those early days I was more amazed and fascinated. I already enjoyed doing network programming and HTTP reasoned with me at once.

httpget 0.1 was almost completely without error checks and it used plain IPv4 addresses; no hostnames or URLs.

I, still a naive and enthusiastic developer with an Open Source mindset (even though that term would not be established until 15-16 months later), addressed some immediate bugs I ran into and added name resolving to the tool. I made diffs and emailed patches over to Rafael; the standard way we exchanged code changes back then. I knew about RCS and CVS for version control, but the use of these tools was spotty. It would actually take until September 1999 until I adopted CVS fully for the curl project. We later switched to using git in 2010.

The average internet connection speed of a normal household in Sweden, where I lived and I still live, in 1996 was 30 kbps. 30 kilobit per second. This was before v90 came and bumped the modems up to 56 kilobits. Ordinary mortals connected to the internet using modems over their single phone lines. Today, the average Swedish connection speed is 200 megabits/second.

Thirty years ago there were just 36 million global Internet users and 250,000 websites. Compared to the 6 or 7 billion users and 1 billion websites of today.

We used simpler protocols and while encrypted protocols like SSL existed, they were not used a lot and only for a few rare sites.

In November 1996, my main home computer was still an Amiga 3000 powered by a 25Mhz 68030 CPU but in early 1997 I upgraded to a faster and more modern machine: an Intel Pentium 120Mhz. I ran Windows 95 on this thing, and its prime use was to run an X server so that I could connect to my work computers and pop up X11 terminals at home. I built the first versions of httpget remotely on SunOS, Solaris and Dell Unix – because they happened to be what we had running at work.

I installed and tested Linux for the first time at work in 1997. I got our first public web servers up and of course I made sure curl worked fine on it. I did not switch to Linux on my home machine until 2000 when I also updated to an Intel Pentium III 733 Mhz box.

In 1996 I was working as a software developer doing embedded systems and Unix development in C, for a small Swedish company called Frontec Railway Systems. While working there, I came to learn about and enjoy IRC, and in my spare time a few friends and I developed an IRC bot we called Dancer. Spare time developing a TCP client written in C.

As the IRC bot slowly grew more capable, I wanted to use its extension capability and provide a currency translation service for the participants in the channel (the IRC term for a chat room). In an international channel like ours, we frequently discussed the price of things and having the bot able to quickly explain how much a hundred German Marks equaled in US Dollars could be a useful service.

My currency service needed to update currency rates maybe once per day so that it could use decently accurate rates. I found an HTTP page listing a bunch of currency rates and the httpget tool for doing the downloads, and then the bot could offer up-to-date currency rate translations. All was good.

I discovered computers and programming as a teenager on a Commodore 64. I got hooked immediately. I first learned Basic and moved on to 6510 assembler pretty quickly. In the late 1980s me and my friends had demo groups where we would write cool demos (and some game attempts) in assembler (under the group name Horizon). I established my habit of spending spare time on programming back then.

In the early 1990s I moved over to Amiga, started writing a text editor, got my first job at IBM where I truly got into a lot of C and Unix for the first time. Together with some friends we ran a BBS (The Holy Grail), for which we eventually would write our own BBS software; me and my brother Björn. I learned Motorola 68000 assembler on the Amiga. I wrote 8086 assembler on PC.

I never attended university. I got my first computer job at IBM when I was twenty. I then thought I would take the uni route later, but I never did. I remain uneducated.

In the early 1990s I discovered both the Internet and the world of freely available source code and I was hooked.

Rafael was not terribly keen on dealing with my patches for httpget. I believe he mostly just put his code out without any particular desire to do anything more with it. Instead I became the httpget maintainer and kept polishing it. My main project was Dancer, the IRC bot. httpget was just a side-project to make sure the currency service kept working fine.

At some point I fell over a gopher site that provided many more currency rates than the HTTP page I was scraping at the time so of course I had to add support for that as well to the download tool. With gopher support added, it was not just http anymore and the name of the tool was no longer accurate. It became urlget. A third listing was found that provided rates over FTP and, yes, I added support for that protocol as well.

Already from the start I made the source code available under a free license, continuing what Rafel kicked off. He hosted the first releases, but during 1997 I took over and hosted the tarballs on the website I set up and administrated for work. I told my friends and the news about the tool slowly spread. I started getting bug reports from users and occasionally someone sent me patches to fix problems or add features.

This was a time of many Unix flavors and as I wanted widest possible use and adoption, I knew that I needed help and assistance from friends to make sure it built and ran fine on all those different systems.

In the beginning of 1998 I added upload support to the urlget tool (both FTP upload and HTTP POST) and again I realized the name of the tool was wrong. I decided I should try a name that contains the word URL, that can be pronounced in English and that is easy (and short) to type on a keyboard. cURL it was.

The leading ‘c’ could be short for client but I also liked that the name could be pronounced as see URL, as the tool would display the resource at the URL. You would see it (in a terminal). Naming things is hard.

curl 4.0 was released on March 20, 1998. By then it had grown to 3,300 lines of code and it featured 24 command line options and it spoke three protocols.

Gradually I lost interest in the IRC bot and the currency service but I stuck with curl. People used it, I got feedback, it improved.

I started and participated in several other Open Source projects, but curl remained my main baby and focus.

The concept of a function library that offers useful functionality to other programs is a concept I learned already on my Amiga days. As an example, I wrote the scripting language (FPL) for our Amiga text editor (FrexxEd) as a library, and we could later use that language for our BBS software, FrexxLink (which ran on OS/2) as well as in Dancer, the IRC bot.

A library is sort of next-level cool: not only is the source code available for everyone, but the functionality is as well; in an easy-to-use way.

The idea of converting curl into a library was already in the back of head from the start and in the summer of 2000 I refactored the internals and in August that year we introduced the first ever libcurl. Maybe someone else wants to do Internet transfers in their services or tools? Turns out some did!

One of the first adopters of libcurl was the PHP language which almost immediately decided that libcurl would become their default internet transfer engine. Being a key component and therefore part of their success journey helped getting users, getting testing, bug reports, feature requests and making the library solid.

curl is a child of the 1990s. Back then there were not a lot of options and language alternatives if you wanted to write a program that would easily build and run on most available operating systems and CPU architectures. Sure, C++ maybe could have been an option but I never liked it – and I still don’t. I’m also a strong believer in continuous and non-stop improvements and iterations; not rewrites. curl was never rewritten and if I get my way, it never will be. We do however repeatedly refactor and rearchitect internals to adapt to a changing world.

I wanted curl to be usable by everyone on every machine so it was designed and written for that purpose from the start. The source code in a portable way and the license in a liberal way.

We did most things wrong at the beginning but we learned, adapted, tried again, iterated and we kept doing release after release. Gradually we learned and did better. Every release with lots of bugs fixed and often a few new features. I kept spending my spare time on curl. Every day, every week, every year. Given enough time, something great can grow.

I did my first twenty-three years of this journey with curl only as my hobby. While curl happened, life also happened in parallel. I have switched jobs many times. I got married, bought a house, got two kids, and saw the kids grow up to be amazing adults. Somewhere in there I also managed to convert my hobby into my full time job. Living the dream.

curl is my life. My life is curl. I have been invited and able to speak to audiences hundreds of times in a dozen countries. I have received multiple awards and even gold medals straight from the hands of royalties for my open source work.

I don’t have an end goal with curl and I never did. I just want it to do internet transfers the best way possible: fast, securely, using the proper protocols in optimal ways. There is no rush towards anything. It is just a non-stop walk forward with never-ending polish and tightening every bolt there is.

Thirty years have flown by and yet the development pace is still intense. We regularly implement new transfer protocol features before anyone else. We have leading implementations for lots of network solutions. We ship code that carries a huge portion of the world’s internet infrastructure on its shoulders without fuss.

I still enjoy building things. Writing code to create something that did not exist before; and maybe even more so to make the program actually do things users want and like. I enjoy fixing bugs partly for that reason, but I also like the puzzle and the challenge of debugging and solving tricky problems. Designing a software architecture, coming up with APIs and figuring out how to provide powerful network transfer functionality to power billions of devices are things that make me eager to get started again every morning – still after thirty years.

It never really gets done. The world of the Internet and its transfers keeps changing. New protocols, new versions, new flavors, new third party libraries, new build tools and environments force us to constantly change and adapt.

I want curl to be a leader in internet transfers, its protocol implementations and every aspect of the project. I want us to be an exemplary Open Source project and run every tiny piece of it in an almost excessively transparent and progressive way. curl should be a top contender for the most-secure software component you can find. Our project should be friendly and welcoming to newcomers, both users and developers and not the least, there can be no other software project to compete with the amount, the accuracy and the plethora of documentation. Not to mention that we never break APIs or ABIs. Applications and scripts should be able to keep running, unmodified, even when they upgrade curl. Until the end of times.

I’m a firm believer in iterating and never rewriting. We fix, we refactor and we clean up but rewriting into another language or even using the same language is out of the question.

Simply put: software engineering done right.

While curl speaks more than two dozen protocols (at least counting URL schemes), it has always been most known for HTTP(S) and I think we put the most work and efforts into its HTTP engine. We know lots of people use curl for debugging HTTP in general and their server implementations in particular. We were early adopters of both HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. We are often told people use our way of speaking HTTP and our source code as guidance for how things should be done. This is an honor and a huge responsibility that we take seriously.

After I first had learned about HTTP from reading httpget source code and then of course studied the RFC documentation explaining the specifics. In the late 2000s I learned about the HTTPbis effort and joined the mailing list for the HTTP specification update in the works. In 2009 I participated in my first ever IETF meeting that took place in Stockholm, Sweden. There, I got to meet some of the HTTP RFC authors and main people for the first time: Roy, Larry, Mark, Julian etc. They are all lovely people and I really felt that I would be able to make curl better by hanging out in the HTTP IETF circles more. I also wanted to contribute back my own experiences and viewpoints to maybe help improve the world ever so slightly.

That community later started the HTTP Workshop series out of which I have been to every single instance. Hanging out with the primary HTTP implementers in the world is fun, super educational and humbling. I believe this networking makes HTTP and all the involved  implementations even better.

curl is not a legal entity or a formal organization of any kind. It is a bunch of loosely connected people on the Internet who have a common goal, a few mailing lists, a website and some git repositories. curl is not hosted under any umbrella, not part of any larger organization and is not owned or controlled by any company. It is probably as free and independent as a software project can be. I believe this is an excellent position for curl and gives us maximum flexibility and control of our own destiny.

libcurl runs in an estimated thirty billion installations today. It is a rough estimate since the majority of all libcurl users never tell us they use it, but we need to find it mentioned in their credit screens, open source license windows or their manuals. A super popular app might use libcurl today and not tomorrow, or vice versa, which can make the numbers shift by several billions overnight. In reality of course, once the pulse raise has calmed down and your ego is content, these numbers do not matter. In our corner of the world, things don’t change notably when we go from a thousand installs to billions. We still work with similar people, in similar ways, with similar challenges.

For me, and for many others, the coolest place curl has been used is probably on Mars. It was confirmed by NASA that curl was used to aid the Mars landing mission, even if they don’t tell us exactly for what and where.

A ridiculously common question to me is “what is the weirdest place you’ve seen curl run?” I have ceased getting surprised about what devices and what things that are Internet connected and thus where curl runs. Light-bulbs, dish washers, AC units, heat pumps, cars, printers, blenders, ovens, toy robots, drones, guns, motorcycles, medical devices, fridges, soundbars and espresso machines. Of course in addition to all those “traditional” things we already expect to run curl: games, servers, cars, printers, TVs, watches, tablets, game consoles, blue-tooth speakers, routers, mobile phone apps and their operating systems.

Our modern society is keen at eventually making everything network connected, and once they are, they can use curl and libcurl to perform their transfers.

Benevolent Dictator For Life. A term popularly used to describe the steering mechanism of many Open Source projects. Basically a single person being the captain of the ship. The one who can commandeer the direction, who can dictate truths about the project and who says yes and no firmly. For better and for worse, I remain the BDFL for curl. I try to repeat that curl is not a solo-show and it was never a one-man circus. We are literally thousands of people who have contributed code, and every year there are hundreds of new authors helping out. I may remain the captain of the ship, but no ship above a certain size can be managed without a lot of additional man power and curl is no different.

I may very well remain BDFL for a long time to come because I love my role and because I don’t know any other way to live my life or to run the curl project. There are no succession plans and I am against doing such. There is no heir or vice-BDFL prepared to take over. Instead we document everything and every detail so there are no secrets, so that no formal hand-over should be necessary (except for some rare passwords). If I get run over by a truck tomorrow, you guys can figure it out and continue. You don’t need me.

My email address is commonly listed in the regular curl license and this license is usually included in license listings, credit screens or manuals. When random people run into problems or issues with products in this modern society, they often struggle to find someone to help them. There is no one to contact or ask. My email then sometimes serves as a last resort to finally get the answers they’ve been fighting for. I frequently get emails about products I never knew existed, I certainly didn’t know they used curl and I for sure don’t know how to help the users with their problems…

The much darker side of the traces curl usage leaves in products, is when malicious tools, services and attackers use tools that can be associated with me and my email address. I have been accused of various attacks and “hacking” people and companies multiple times. I have received death threats multiple times and I strongly suspect that my US visa problems were triggered by something in these veins.

I stick to the Open Source ethos and spirit. It is a fundamental part of my belief system and I am convinced this is the superior way to produce software to build society on. I do everything I can to stick to the liberal license curl is shipped under because I love the concept. It is however not an easy pitch: give everything away for free and then try to get someone to pay for it. I think it is fair to say that if I wanted to optimize for money, I should have played this one out differently. That would have been another life. Not my life.

Of course I feel immensely proud of what we have accomplished. The little toy thing in 1996 kicked off a journey that led to the creation and continued maintenance of a modern Internet infrastructure cornerstone. We have reached this point, not by talking, not by using marketing nor by tricking someone into using our code. We conquered the world by shipping consistent top quality over several decades. curl runs in all these devices and services done by all those companies because it is the right choice for them, selected because it is Open Source, rock-solid and fast – and also likely to be around in the future. Everyone can depend on us to keep shipping updates in a proven stellar fashion and minimal friction. Forever and ever.

There are many dimensions of the future to consider here. The future of Open Source. The future of curl. The future of internet transfers. The future of the C programming language and the future for me, personally. At least.

I don’t think I can guess the future any better than other humans. I was never good at it and I never really tried to. I always only focus on the next coming months and make quick adjustments when things make turns.

I think Open Source is a solid way to do foundational software, now and in the future. It will continue to have a funding problem and too many projects live and die with a single maintainer. But building common and open building blocks is simply a requirement for speedy development, for building reliable components and for being able to produce products and services at the speed we seem to want. I don’t believe AI will kill Open Source.

I think curl has many more years of service ahead. Primarily because it is the trusted solution and nothing else is even close to this long proven track record, secondarily because it runs on all platforms like no alternatives. I do not rule out that it will be replaced by an alternative at some point, when projects written in C are gradually phased out. (If they ever are.)

Internet transfers in general seem like a fundamental idea that probably is going to be around in a similar style for a long time. The protocols will keep evolving, changing and getting updated but the client/server/protocol concept seems solid and likely to be here for the long term.

I personally will keep working on curl and Internet transfers for as long as I think it is fun and challenging. I turn 56 years old in a few weeks. I hope to be able to spend several more decades on this.

#9991. Security incident disclosure — July 2026

Earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure. This one was different from anything we had handled before in one important way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system - and we detected and dissected it largely with AI of our own.

We identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and to several credentials used by our services. We are still completing our assessment of whether any partner or customer data was affected, and we will contact any affected parties directly as required. We have found no evidence of tampering with public, user-facing models, datasets, or Spaces, and our software supply chain (container images and published packages) was verified clean.

The intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline. A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths in our dataset processing (a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration) to run code on a processing worker. From there, the actor escalated to node-level access, harvested cloud and cluster credentials, and moved laterally into several internal clusters over a weekend.

The campaign was run by an autonomous agent framework (appearing to be built on an agentic security-research harness - used LLM still not known) executing many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services. This matches the "agentic attacker" scenario the industry has been forecasting.

We are working with outside cybersecurity forensic specialists to investigate the issue and review our security policies and procedures. Finally, we have also reported this incident to law enforcement agencies.

As a precaution, we recommend rotating any access tokens and reviewing recent activity on your account. If you believe you are affected, or want to report a security concern, contact us at security@huggingface.co.

We are grateful to the teams across Hugging Face who responded around the clock, and we are sorry for any disruption this caused. Security is never finished; we will keep raising the bar.

The attack was initially surfaced through AI-assisted detection. Our anomaly-detection pipeline uses LLM-based triage over security telemetry to separate real signals from the daily noise, and it was the correlation of those signals that flagged the compromise.

To understand what a swarm of tens of thousands of automated actions did, we ran LLM-driven analysis agents over the full attacker action log, comprised of more than 17,000 recorded events. This allowed us to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, map the credentials touched, and separate genuine impact from decoy activity. Thanks to this approach, we were able to do in hours what would usually take days, and match the adversary's speed.

The choice of models we could use for this analysis was constrained in a way we did not anticipate; we describe this below.

When we started the log analysis, we first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers' safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker. We ran the forensic analysis instead on zai-org/GLM-5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment.

This experience points to a gap worth planning for. We do not know which model powered the attacker's agents, whether a jailbroken hosted model or an unrestricted open-weight one; either way, the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried. The practical lesson for defenders: have a capable model you can run on your own infrastructure vetted and ready before an incident, both to avoid guardrail lockout and to keep attacker data and credentials from leaving your environment. This is not an argument against safety measures on hosted models, and we are sharing this feedback with the providers concerned.

Autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical. It lowers the cost of running a broad, patient, multi-stage campaign, and it operates at machine speed. Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defense to keep pace. We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn.

#9990. Another contract extension for Fujitsu on the Post Office's Horizon

Just a few more months until Accenture takes over running scandal-hit Horizon system

The UK Post Office is extending its contract with Fujitsu to give it time to move services to a new supplier, after a scandal that has long marred the relationship between the two.

The current contract runs until March 2027, and the publicly owned company has announced a short, time-limited contract extension to cover the transition.

Accenture will take over running the Horizon system, which was at the center of a string of miscarriages of justice, from September 2027, after winning a £410 million contract in May this year. Meanwhile, the Post Office is developing a replacement for the aging system to serve its network of 11,500 branches.

The Post Office began rolling out the legacy Horizon IT system for accounting in 1999, along with two subsequent upgrades. The electronic point-of-sale (EPOS) and back-end finance system was first implemented by ICL, a UK tech firm majority-owned by Fujitsu in the 1990s and which it fully acquired in 1998. From 1999 until 2015, around 736 subpostmasters were wrongfully prosecuted and convicted over Horizon errors, devastating lives in the process.

The Post Office, Accenture, and Fujitsu have agreed that Fujitsu will hand over the operation of Horizon to Accenture between 1 June and 1 September 2027, with the final date set to be confirmed in March 2027.

Accenture is set to "walk in and take over" the current Horizon system by assuming day-to-day operations from Fujitsu, as well as developing the back-end of the new system to replace Horizon.

Post Office CEO Neil Brocklehurst said: "Ending our contract with Fujitsu is a critical milestone in Post Office's transformation, and today's agreement secures the transition away from Fujitsu and over to Accenture safely and responsibly to achieve our target of summer 2027.

"In addition to ending our contract with Fujitsu, we are also working at pace with our leading technology suppliers, Accenture, OneView Commerce, and Escher, to build a modern, resilient platform able to make everyday life easier for customers and postmasters for years to come."

Fujitsu has also been awarded a contract extension to run the UK Government's Emergency Alerts platform until October 2029. The contract is worth £9.6 million ($12.8 million).

The company committed to not bid for new public sector contracts while the inquiry into the Horizon scandal continues.    ®

#9988. Newer Models, Same Advantage

Three months ago, we published a paper on DharmaOCR and open-sourced one of the models. The objective was specific: optical character recognition engineered for Brazilian Portuguese.

The training pipeline was built in two stages. The first was a supervised fine-tuning step, drawing on a broad collection of Portuguese-language files from different sources, formats, and levels of complexity. This stage aligned the model's weights to the specific vocabulary, syntax, and document structures of Brazilian Portuguese — concentrating representational capacity on the target language rather than distributing it across a broader multilingual space. The second stage applied Direct Preference Optimization: rather than training only on correct transcriptions, the model learned from comparative preference data between competing outputs, teaching it to consistently select the better extraction at inference time. This stage addressed a different problem: not accuracy, but stability. By suppressing the failure modes that cause generative models to produce repetitive or incoherent output, DPO reduced inference time and cost, and materially improved the reliability of what the model delivered in production.

The combined result was a model that achieved the highest extraction quality score with the lowest degeneration rate on a Portuguese-focused benchmark. Both stages were necessary. The fine-tuning stage built domain competency; the DPO stage ensured that competency held under the conditions where models tend to fail.

OCR models have been moving quickly. But the gaps that originally motivated DharmaOCR's design (in extraction quality on complex documents and in model stability under production conditions) have not closed. They have, if anything, become more instructive as the field has changed.

The proliferation of multimodal generative models made language model-based OCR widely accessible, and the wave of fine-tuned OCR variants that followed reflects how fast that adoption has moved. That proliferation has not, however, changed the fundamental character of the technology. Every OCR system built on a generative model is probabilistic. Transcription errors are an inherent variable of this probabilistic technology. What differentiates models is how many errors they make and of what kind. That is determined by two things: the structure of the model (its architecture and parameter count) and how those parameters were trained for the task.

Architecture and parameter count establish the ceiling on what a model can learn. Training determines how that capacity is allocated.

This distinction is where specialization becomes a structural question rather than a design preference. When a model is trained on a restricted domain — a single language, a bounded document type, a specific task — All of its parameters are dedicated to that specific task. When a model is trained to cover a broader range of domains — a multilingual model handling N languages, for instance — those same parameters must be distributed across all of them. The distribution is not linear: the neuron superposition principle means individual parameters can encode multiple features simultaneously. But the division is real, and its consequences are real. A model covering more ground commits less to any given part of it.

DharmaOCR was trained to accept that constraint in reverse. The model is not designed to be the best option for other languages, and was never intended to be. In exchange, every parameter available to the network could be oriented toward the specific vocabulary, morphology, and orthographic patterns of Brazilian Portuguese — the most directed possible use of the model's resources for that domain.

That concentration is the structural basis of an inherent advantage over multilingual and broader-domain models. The advantage does not depend on having a larger architecture or a more sophisticated training procedure than competitors use — new architectures and new training techniques improve what any model can do. It depends on where those resources are directed: at one domain rather than spread across many.

Three months later, newer models have arrived. Whether the case for specialization holds when those models are newer and more capable is a different question.

Three months after the DharmaOCR paper appeared, two new OCR models attracted significant attention from the research community: Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR. Both represent genuine technical advances — new training techniques, new datasets, and strong results across multiple languages on a range of benchmark evaluations. They are the kind of models that raise the competitive standard for what OCR systems are expected to deliver.

When we ran both against the DharmaOCR benchmark — an evaluation designed exclusively around Portuguese — the results were conclusive.

DharmaOCR scored 0.925. Mistral OCR4 scored 0.798. Unlimited-OCR scored 0.7587.

The difference is significant. Mistral OCR4 falls approximately 13 points below DharmaOCR; Unlimited-OCR falls more than 16 points below. Both were released after our model, both backed by substantial research resources. On a task where DharmaOCR's fundamental design decision was to concentrate entirely on Portuguese, the specialization advantage is measurable and significant.

The benchmark is the central finding. What follows illustrates why the gap takes the specific shape it does.

Processing non-trivial Portuguese documents reveals precisely where multilingual models tend to break. ENEM essays (Brazil's national high school examination) combine handwritten text with vocabulary, proper nouns, and cultural references that are specific to Brazilian Portuguese. They are exactly the kind of documents where language-specific training produces a return.

Figure 1: ENEM essay manuscript used in benchmark evaluation with outputs of the each model. Misreads marked in red.

Mistral OCR4, evaluated on documents of this kind, transcribed the name Chico Buarque (one of Brazil's most widely recognized musicians and poets) as "Chico Barque." Unlimited-OCR rendered the same name as "chico bique." Confronted with the phrase "O Brasil não exclui, assimila" ("Brazil does not exclude, it assimilates", a Chico Buarque quotation embedded in the same document) Unlimited-OCR returned: "a dose de chico bique, 'o Brasil no exclu, eliminila.'

These are not random errors. A model with insufficient exposure to Brazilian Portuguese does not fail arbitrarily — it fails at precisely the vocabulary and proper nouns that distinguish Brazilian Portuguese from the broader multilingual corpus. Chico Buarque is not an obscure reference; the name is nationally recognized. Its systematic corruption across outputs is not an edge case. It is a diagnostic: evidence of where the model's training did not go.

DharmaOCR, evaluated on the same documents, handles these cases correctly. The reason is direct: the model's training was concentrated on this linguistic space, orienting its resources toward the vocabulary and proper noun distributions that characterize Brazilian Portuguese rather than spreading them across many languages at once.

The examples illustrate the benchmark rather than replace it. The benchmark establishes the magnitude of the gap; the examples show why it is concentrated in language-specific recognition rather than in general capability.

Extraction accuracy, however, is only one dimension of production performance. Stability under visual difficulty is another — and operationally, it is the more consequential one to fail on.

When a generative model encounters a document it cannot clearly resolve — small fonts, degraded scan quality, dense handwriting — it faces uncertainty in its input signal. Models trained primarily on next-token prediction objectives face a specific vulnerability here: when the visual signal becomes ambiguous, the model can continue generating from prior learned patterns rather than from the source document. The result is text degeneration — output that is repetitive, incoherent, and semantically disconnected from the page.

Presented with a document with small fonts, Mistral OCR4 produces output with no connection to what is written.

Figure 3: DharmaOCR output and Mistral OCR4 degenerated output

This is not a low-quality transcription of the source. It is a failure of an entirely different category.

The operational consequence is distinct from that of a transcription error. An incorrect transcription is wrong in a recoverable way — it stands in a relationship to the source document, and the error can in principle be identified and corrected. Degenerated output has no such relationship. It cannot be corrected because there is nothing to correct toward. For downstream processes that depend on structured OCR output — document classification, information extraction, compliance workflows — degenerated output is not inaccurate data. It is structurally unusable data. The efficiency that automation was meant to deliver is negated at precisely the point where output stops being information.

Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR are good models with significant technical advances behind them. The degeneration behavior described here does not define them; it identifies a specific failure condition that their current training has not addressed for this domain. The question is what a training pipeline designed to address it looks like.

In DharmaOCR, the answer is the DPO stage.

Supervised fine-tuning concentrates the model's resources on the target domain — the stage that builds the linguistic alignment described above. But SFT trains on individual token predictions: the model learns to produce the correct next token given the context preceding it. Under visual complexity, this creates the condition that produces degeneration. If an early token in the output diverges from the source document, each subsequent prediction is conditioned on that divergent state, and the output continues to drift. Repetition loops and incoherent sequences are an inherent characteristic in this context — they are the predictable result of an objective optimized step by step without accounting for the coherence of the full extraction.

DPO trains against a different signal. Where SFT trains token by token, DPO trains the model against the quality of complete outputs — teaching it to discriminate between competing responses based on the coherence of the full extraction rather than the accuracy of individual predictions. The effect is stabilizing: on documents where visual complexity would otherwise trigger drift, the model is less likely to commit to a divergent path, because its training penalized outputs that lost coherence at the extraction level.

The result is what the original benchmark demonstrated: lower degeneration rates alongside higher extraction accuracy, on the same documents where models without this training stage lose coherence.

The benchmark establishes what is true today. It is less precise about what will be true in two years.

It is possible — and likely — that newer models will eventually outperform the current DharmaOCR even in Brazilian Portuguese. Architectures will improve. Training techniques will advance. Datasets will expand. The field moves toward higher capability at every level, and there is no reason to expect that trajectory to stop. This is expected, and it is welcome.

What changes with each architectural generation is the ceiling on absolute performance. What does not change is the structural logic that determines which systems come closest to their ceiling in a given domain.

Available resources — compute, parameters, training data — are finite. They must be directed somewhere. A system that directs them at a single domain will extract more from them in that domain than a system distributing the same resources across many. This relationship holds regardless of how capable the generalist model has become. The gap between specialist and generalist may evolve as architectures improve. The structural dynamic does not reverse. We explored this principle in more depth in an earlier piece on why specialization continues to produce an advantage as AI systems advance (Why Specialization Is Inevitable).

This is what shapes how Dharma approaches what comes next. The objective is not to defend the current model's benchmark position. It is to remain at the frontier of emerging techniques — new architectures, new training methods, new approaches to alignment and evaluation — and adapt them toward the same end: a specialized system for Brazilian Portuguese OCR that makes the best possible use of available resources, at the lowest possible cost and the shortest possible inference time.

Better tools do not work against specialization. They expand what it can achieve.

Three months ago, we showed that concentrating a model's training on a specific domain produces a measurable advantage over generalist systems, including ones that are newer and better-resourced. That advantage held. The same principle will determine how DharmaOCR continues to evolve — not by staying fixed, but by applying whatever progress the field makes to a domain that remains fixed.

#9987. Fireworks AI gets burned twice as customer data exposure widens

Inference biz pins latest breach on cloud provider and LLMJacking miscreants

Fireworks AI has disclosed another cyberattack in October and a wider customer data exposure involving billing records, datasets, and incomplete model weights.

The company, which lets customers train and run AI models, said a third-party cloud provider hosting its research and development machines was compromised on October 23. Attackers used that access the following day to reach Fireworks development systems and run an unauthorized workload.

Fireworks suspects links to financially motivated criminals involved in LLMJacking – selling unauthorized access to AI models through illicit gateways.

Fireworks grouped the affected data into three categories:

Resource metadata: Resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, creation times, and more

Billing information: Billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment histories, account balances, and credit usages. Payment card numbers are not saved and therefore unaffected

Model weights and datasets: For certain customers, a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets were accessed, Fireworks said

Lin Qiao, Fireworks co-founder and CEO, said the apparent motive was not stealing model weights in response to concerns raised by Cantina Security CEO Hari Mulackal.

"From what we see attackers are not after weights," said Qiao. "Most downloads were partial and stopped."

Render founder and CEO Anurag Goel shared a notification from Notion warning that some chats with its AI assistant may have been exposed through the Fireworks incident.

"Following an investigation by the Notion security team, we have determined that your workspace, Render, was among the <1 percent of Notion workspaces that may have been affected by the Fireworks security incident," the email sent to Goel stated.

"Some unattributable chat sessions with Notion AI may have been exposed in this incident."

Notion said the exposed transcripts lacked separate information linking them to particular users or workspaces. As Reddit users pointed out, however, the conversations themselves could contain identifying details.

"Beyond what's in the chat transcript itself, there's no information tying the chat back to your workspace, users, or company," the email added. "No other data from within your workspace is affected."

Bloomberg reports that Fireworks is also working with customers including Cursor and Harvey to assess the impact.

Fireworks' update confirmed that it worked with Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 team to remediate the attack, which included rotating credentials, isolating affected systems from the network, and tightening up data storage access and monitoring systems.

The update did not state how many customers were affected by either of the two attacks in October.

Fireworks first disclosed an incident on October 9 after detecting unauthorized use of internal credentials on October 6. Attackers accessed environment variables in evaluation jobs, including API keys and tokens belonging to some customers.

At the time, Fireworks said it had found no evidence of access to models, datasets, training data, inference traffic, or personal information. Monday's update substantially broadens the disclosed impact. ®

#9986. Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers

Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms.

The dock that he was trying to support is a Dell device that connects to a system via USB 3 and allows users to connect multiple monitors and other devices to their computer. It provides its DisplayLink Manager (DLM) software for Linux for the devices via an APT repository for Ubuntu.

The company only provides DLM software in binary form, and only for x86-based platforms. The software is proprietary, but the company does maintain an open-source, out-of-tree kernel module that is included with DLM, the Extensible Virtual Display Interface (EVDI) project. It provides a driver that's compatible with Linux DRM and allows users to manage their docked displays with standard tools used for display settings, such as xrandr or GNOME and KDE Plasma's utilities.

A short article explains why the company has not released source code for DLM: the software uses a proprietary graphics technology called DL3 to create a compressed stream of the various channels (e.g., USB, DisplayLink video, audio) over a communication channel (USB 3 in this case) and decode it again for output to the user's devices.

Unfortunately, the vendor-supplied software did not work well for Lothian. I spoke and chatted with him via Signal while writing this article; he said that the driver kept crashing under Linux, so he decided to use his Claude subscription to try to develop a new driver and support software.

He posted the first patch series for Vino—his Rust-based DRM/KMS driver—to the kernel's dri-devel list as an RFC on June 17. Lothian noted that it was in an incomplete state, and asked for help with a blocker that he had run into trying to communicate with the dock's control plane. "If you have knowledge of the DisplayLink DL3 control-plane engagement sequence, or ideas for isolating a whole-bus timing/ordering property a per-channel diff cannot see, help would be very welcome." He received feedback from a few developers, including guidance from Danilo Krummrich to rework the driver to use the Rust KMS bindings, but no advice specific to the problem he was trying to solve.

Lothian also opened an issue on the EVDI GitHub repository on June 17. It explained the work he'd done so far, outlined the approach in trying to reverse-engineer the DL3 protocol, provided links to his GitHub repository with the Vino code, and asked for clarification on a few issues. There was no reply to his issue.

He also reached out to Łukasz Spintzyk of Synaptics directly by email; his correspondence with the company between July 5 and October 7 is available in this PDF compiled by Lothian. He noted that he had found a few bugs in EVDI and opened a pull request (that went unreviewed for several months), and also asked for assistance where he was blocked on Vino. On July 20, he received a reply, not from Spintzyk, but from Michal Lukaszek of Synaptics:

The reason I'm writing is that DisplayLink is not an open standard. The protocol, codec, and other technologies used by DisplayLink devices are proprietary to Synaptics and are protected by a substantial portfolio of patents in a number of jurisdictions, including the UK.

From what you've published, it appears that the VINO project is progressing beyond interoperability work and toward implementing technology that we believe is covered by those patents. While many developers understandably focus on avoiding copyrighted source code, patent law is different. An independently written or clean-room implementation does not necessarily avoid patent infringement if it implements patented inventions.

Lukaszek said it was entirely possible that Lothian was unaware of the "intellectual property landscape surrounding DisplayLink", so he wanted to make him aware now rather than "have the situation become more formal later". Lothian lives in Scotland and has a ".co.uk" email address, which explains why the email made reference to the UK.

On August 17, Andrew Bateman, an assistant general council of intellectual property for Synaptics, sent a cease-and-desist notice. The letter stated that Lothian had not "substantially responded" to Lukaszek's communication, and had continued with "public statements and further development activities". It included an appendix with a list of 125 patents that "cover fundamental aspects of DisplayLink's architecture and operation", but did not specify which patents might be infringed by the work.

Synaptics included a list of eight demands it expected immediate compliance with, including ceasing development of "any software or other implementation that infringes any Synaptics patent", withdrawing submissions of materials "made to Linux kernel maintainers, mailing lists, code-hosting platforms, package maintainers, distributions, or any other person or organization", and to identify in writing every location "in which the relevant materials have been published, submitted, stored, or distributed". It also demanded that he provide Synaptics with a signed confirmation, by August 28, that he had complied with its demands.

Lothian, instead, posted version three of his Vino work for the DisplayLink docks to the dri-devel list on August 26. He said that the previous two versions had "never lit a panel", but the new work could control three generations of DL3 docks without any vendor software. There were no substantive reviews of the patch set posted to the list, though there were some automated reviews from Sashiko.

On August 27, Lothian responded to Bateman and asked him to elaborate on the patents that Synaptics thought were being infringed. "A claim chart mapping the relevant claims to the relevant code would make it much easier for me to understand and properly respond to your concerns."

He also expressed confusion about Synaptics's position that his work was being treated as patent infringement. Synaptics is a member of the Open Invention Network (OIN), which was created to help open-source developers and vendors deal with the threats of expensive patent litigation. It holds a large, cross-licensed portfolio that serves to provide patent protection to individuals, open-source projects, and large vendors alike. Lothian said that he was now an OIN licensee as well, and he thought that it was supposed to "reduce exactly this sort of patent problem around Linux and open source software".

Lothian did not think he could "reasonably provide the signed undertaking" Synaptics had demanded by August 28 without understanding which patent claims it was alleging. He asked for an extension to the deadline. There was no response from Bateman, so Lothian sent a follow-up email on September 18. He said he was concerned there was no acknowledgment to his last email, and wondered it was safe to assume he could continue his work. He had been running the Vino driver himself for quite a while, and was eager to move it upstream without having patent threats hanging over the work.

Bateman responded the next day and said that he should be concerned:

The letter continued to claim that Lothian would be "single-handedly eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our proprietary technology". He said that DisplayLink is not a member of OIN, and none of its technology is licensable through OIN or any other organization.

Bateman sent a follow-up letter, dated October 5, that included two claim charts for UK patents: GB2484736B ("Display control device") and GB2485613B ("Image generation"), both filed in 2010 and published in 2012. He reiterated Synaptics's demands from its previous letter, and said that the deadline was now October 11; failure to comply would result in the company seeking "monetary compensation from you in the amount of US$25,000 to recoup the costs and effort required to create the attached documentation of your infringing acts". That amount would be increased by $25,000 each week until the company's demands were complied with.

Lothian responded the next day, by email, to say that he was on vacation, and would not be back home until October 13. He asked for an extension of the deadline to return home and go through the claim charts "ideally with someone qualified to help me read them". Bateman replied that Synaptics would agree to extend the deadline to October 18, though no further extensions would be granted. He reiterated that "DisplayLink is not a member of OIN" and none of its technology was licensable through OIN.

Synaptics is a member of OIN, and is listed in the community directory. In addition to joining OIN, Lothian had reached out to the organization to try to solicit its help and has been in communication with some of the staff there. OIN indicated that it would look into the matter and see if he had any protection as an OIN member. That process took longer than Lothian hoped, though OIN did eventually provide its conclusion.

OIN's portfolio covers a wide range of software that matches its Linux System Definition, but it does not cover everything that might be implemented for a Linux system. In particular, its definition specifies that codecs ("a component of a program capable of performing transformations of a video, still image or audio data stream or signal") are not covered unless specifically mentioned in this list of components.

I spoke briefly to OIN CEO Keith Bergelt on October 23, shortly after OIN staff informed Lothian of the result of their research. Bergelt said that OIN's conclusion was that, since codecs are explicitly not covered by OIN's Linux System Definition, its protections did not extend to Lothian's attempted kernel contributions. OIN had recommended that Lothian reach out to a lawyer in the UK, and provided a recommendation.

Unfortunately, that referral did not pan out, Lothian said. He has not given up entirely, but he has taken down the GitHub repository to comply with Synaptics's demands. For now, he may continue working on some of the components that are not affected by the patent claims, but the work on Vino will not be submitted to the kernel. "Vino itself has to remain local until this is sorted out, I just can't afford to defend myself against Synaptics."

Perhaps amusingly, Lothian told me that someone from Synaptics finally replied to the pull request on October 7. Lothian told me he does not intend to follow up on the comments: "You can't threaten to sue me and then say 'can you update your pull request?'"

For the time being, Synaptics has succeeded in shutting down an effort to improve the way DisplayLink docks work with Linux. It is an unpleasant reminder that, while much of the current conversations in open-source communities are concerned with LLM-driven development, software patents still pose problems for free-software developers and users.

So as I understand it, the point behind this displaylink tech, and the reason it's not using displayport, is that it allows you to connect more monitors than the graphics hardware in the computer actually supports. There is a piece of software that runs on the host computer, and acts as a virtual graphics card. The software then sends the display output (compressed in some way) over a regular usb data transport to the dock, which then converts that back into a regular display signal to be sent out over either an hdmi or displayport connector.

Free standard for USB displays is needed Posted Nov 11, 2026 21:10 UTC (Wed) by rgmoore (✭ supporter ✭, #75) [Link] My impression is this is mostly about the "compressed in some way" and "regular USB" parts. Regular USB, even the common variants of USB3, really isn't fast enough for high resolution uncompressed video, so they have to compress it. That's what their "virtual graphics card" does; it's just a video stream compressor. The signal goes over USB to the dock, where it's decompressed and sent to the monitor(s) over DP or HDMI. There might very well be legal problems producing a compatible FOSS implementation if their system uses patent-encumbered compression. It's clearly a second best solution compared to something like Thunderbolt that can handle the uncompressed video stream, but it's better than being restricted to the resolution of video that can be sent over USB uncompressed.

Whatever the patents cover was published as the price of exclusivity (and the two listed ones, filed in 2010, don’t have long left). Whatever they don’t cover is at best a trade secret, and reverse engineering a product you bought is generally a lawful way to learn one. Coke isn't suing the guy on YouTube who fastidiously reverse-engineered Coke. Either way, “showing people how it works” isn’t a harm patent law recognizes. It's a trade-secret grievance smuggled into a patent claim.

In an ideal world it would be immediate invalidation of the patent, because the whole point of patent is precisely to disclose such information — and if they fear that someone may disclose that valuable information then it means patent itself was bogus. In our world… no one cares. Even if it's supposed to invalidate the patent according to law, but in practice you need court decision for that and no one with deep enough pockets is interested in suing Synaptics.

In the USA, patent infringement is covered under USC 271. There are several ways to infringe. Writing open source software isn't one of them: 271(a), direct infringement: Doesn't apply because you're not "making" or "selling" the entire invention. Are you "using" the invention? Well, I don't know: did you just write the code, or did you also run it in an infringing manner? And, if you did just write the code, if you're purely a hobbyist, the "experimental use" defense should cover you. If you do somehow lose on the experimental use exception, and they can prove it's willful, then oh God no! Treble damages! But you know how much treble damages would be for a single unit of a shit product like DisplayLink? Something like $0.60. So you'd probably be able to get the lawsuit thrown out of court based on the de minimis doctrine before it even got to trial. 271(b), inducement: Lots of ways this fails for the plaintiff. One way is that you have to actually talk to the person you're inducing to infringe. So, throw the code over the wall, talk only to other developers and not users, and you're good. 271(c), contributory: You have to sell or offer to sell it. You're not selling anything: you're giving your code away for free. Case closed. 2771(f), extraterritorial: There's a very nice case, Microsoft v. AT&T, where the facts were that Microsoft mailed a copy of Windows to a customer, on a CD or DVD or something like that, and AT&T said, "waaaah, Windoze is a component that infringes our patuntz, so you owe us under 271(f)!" and Microsoft said, "LOL GTFO luzer! Software's intangible and can't be a component of a patented invention!" The Supreme Court agreed with Microsoft. So, yeah, someone in the US should be good to pick up the torch here.

#9985. Grabette: an open system to record robot-manipulation data

Record your own manipulation tasks in minutes with a handheld gripper, turn them into robot-ready datasets automatically, and help grow an open, collaborative dataset for robot learning.

Robot learning has a supply problem. We have capable policy architectures (transformer-based VLAs, diffusion and flow-matching policies, and even world models) and the GPUs to train them. What we lack is large, diverse, real-world manipulation data.

Teleoperating a robot to collect it can be expensive and demanding: first of all, it requires a robot. And depending on the teleoperation method, data collection can be tedious for the user if it takes hours and involve significant hardware and logistical challenges. That is difficult to scale with the wide variety of tasks and environnements required.

But you don't need a robot to collect robot data. Just a human hand, a gripper, a camera, and a way to recover the 6-DoF trajectory of what the hand did. Capture the demonstration and you have data a robot can learn from.

That's what we're releasing today: Grabette, an open, low-cost system for recording manipulation data. Pick it up, record a task with your own hand, and get back a clean, robot-ready dataset. No robot, no lab, no teleop rig.

And that's the bigger goal: if recording a demonstration is as easy as shooting a video, anyone can contribute. We want Grabette to seed a large, open, collaborative manipulation dataset. One no single lab could ever build alone.

Grabette is directly inspired by the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) from Stanford: a handheld gripper with a fisheye camera that records demonstrations "in the wild", recovers camera trajectories with SLAM, and trains visuomotor policies from them.

UMI proved the recipe works. Other (closed source) devices exists like Agibot's MEgo gripper, Genrobot's DAS gripper and Sunday Robotics skill capture glove. Our goal was to make it effortless to use, to get the barrier from "I have a task" to "I have a trained model" as low as possible.

Grabette is built into the modern open ecosystem: LeRobot for datasets, the Hugging Face Hub for sharing, and a processing pipeline you run from your browser with nothing to install. Grabette is something anyone can build on a workbench, use in the field, and contribute data from.

We have been developing Grabette for months, and we feel it has become usable enough to share. We are excited to share it now with you!

Grabette is a handheld gripper instrumented with everything needed to reconstruct a manipulation demonstration.

It carries two cameras, each with a distinct job. Splitting the two roles is deliberate: the cheap wide fisheye gives the policy the context-rich, wrist-camera-style view it needs, while the RGBD camera does the heavy lifting of robust 6-DoF tracking.

And while Grabette records data during tasks performed by a user, it relies on its robotic counterpart to execute the movements it has learned after training. So, meet Gripette, the robotic arm end-effector twin of Grabette.

Grabette hand held recording device (left) and Gripette robot gripper (right)

Components. Standard sensors you can buy, no closed pipeline, no fork lock-in. A Raspberry Pi, a standard Pi camera, an off-the-shelf OAK-D depth camera, magnetic encoders. The whole point is that anyone can build one from parts you can just order.

Robot-agnostic by design. Nothing in the capture or the data format assumes a particular arm. Demonstrations are stored as camera-local 6-DoF cartesian pose plus gripper state, the output is a standard LeRobot dataset on the Hugging Face Hub, so the same data can drive different robots and different learning methods. You will still need the matching Gripette gripper on your arm though.

This release enables anyone to go from "I want to demonstrate a task" to "I have a training-ready dataset" quickly and without prior expertise.

Press the button, and data from the observation camera, the tracking camera (color, depth, and IMU), and the gripper’s encoder joint values are recorded simultaneously, using a single shared clock to ensure proper synchronization. Press the button again to stop the episode, and the data is saved locally on the Raspberry Pi.

Open the Grabette dashboard in your browser. Select the episodes you want to add to the dataset, and with one click, post-processing begins.

Everything is now ready to start training!

A dataset is only interesting if it trains something. So, to show the loop end-to-end, we ship a complete example. But to be clear, this is an example of what is enables, not the product: the release is the recording system. Your Grabette data works with any method that consumes LeRobot datasets.

Our example takes 200 recorded demonstrations such as :

The data bottleneck doesn’t get solved by one lab, but by a community recording demonstrations everywhere. You can now help build the dataset: build a Grabette, record tasks you are interested in, and share them on the Hub. Every episode makes the open dataset bigger and more diverse, and every contributor makes robot learning a little less gated behind expensive hardware.

This release is only the start of the project! Grabette will keep evolving. We already have more coming, including Casquette, a head-mounted POV device to complement Grabette for egocentric capture (still a work in progress). But the most important next step isn’t only ours, it’s also yours: start recording, and let’s build the dataset together.

👉 Build a Grabette (GitHub) · Process your data (HF Space) · Contribute to the dataset

#9984. Trump taps Palantir security chief to run battered US cyber defense agency

Michael LoSapio could inherit a depleted workforce and a political headache or two, courtesy of his current employer

President Donald Trump has nominated Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA, putting an executive from the controversial government supplier in line to run America's civilian cyber defense agency.

The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025.

LoSapio has served as Palantir's CISO since September 2024, having previously led the company's infrastructure and network security team. He first joined the data analytics outfit in 2013, later spent a spell at database company SingleStore, and returned to Palantir in 2017.

If confirmed, LoSapio would move from securing Palantir's systems to leading the federal government's main civilian cyber defense agency. CISA protects federal civilian networks and works with critical infrastructure operators, including power, water, and telecommunications providers.

It's a substantial job, particularly given the state of the agency he would inherit.

CISA has shed more than 1,000 staff, roughly a third of its workforce, since Trump returned to the White House, according to reports. It's now trying to plug the gaps, although acting director Nick Andersen said in September that around 250 would-be recruits were still waiting for security clearance before they could get to work. Andersen has been running CISA since February.

With fewer people to go around, CISA is also rethinking where to spend its time. A strategy published last month emphasizes infrastructure whose failure would do the most damage, raising questions about what gets less attention as the agency operates with fewer staff.

LoSapio would be the second person Trump has put forward for the role. His previous pick, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April after spending more than a year awaiting confirmation, with his nomination becoming caught up in a dispute involving Republican Senator Rick Scott over Coast Guard contracting.

The nomination arrives late in the congressional calendar. If the Senate does not confirm LoSapio before the current Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again for consideration by the incoming Democratic-controlled Senate.

Palantir, co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has become a major supplier of technology to US government agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Its work with immigration authorities has attracted criticism from civil liberties groups and Democratic lawmakers concerned about surveillance and the handling of sensitive personal information.

The controversy isn't confined to the US either. In the UK, WhatsApp messages obtained by campaign group Foxglove this week indicate that Palantir privately lobbied a health minister to consider extending its software into GP patient records, despite that data being expressly excluded from its £330 million NHS England contract for the Federated Data Platform.

That revelation follows news that NHS England wants greater oversight of Palantir's claims about the benefits of its software, amid questions over the evidence supporting its performance figures.

Those controversies could make LoSapio's confirmation hearings particularly interesting, especially as Democrats prepare to scrutinize Palantir's government business more closely.

It's unclear whether LoSapio plans to leave Palantir or what would happen to any financial interests he holds in the company if confirmed. Those are questions likely to come up during a confirmation process that CISA, having spent nearly two years without a permanent boss while losing a third of its workforce, could probably do without dragging on any longer. ®

#9983. The hardest tarball

Personal and work related blogof Harmen Stoppels.

Open source software developerat Stoppels Consultingin Zürich, Switzerland.

Find me on GitHubor send me an email atfirstname[at]lastname.ch

Here is a curiosity: an archive that can be constructed using a single GNU tar invocation, that is extracted in 8 distinct ways depending on what tool you use.

It creates an archive hardest.tar from three files file ./file empty in sequence, where file is repeated so that GNU tar stores the second one as a hard link, and empty is empty. Exploiting the unique path of the second entry, the hard link is renamed to cafÃ©. This triggers tar to create a pax header to store the file name as UTF-8. We add a size=512 record to the pax header, which overrides the default size=0 from the hard link. The value 512 is not a coincidence: it is exactly the size of a tar header.

Visually, this archive has the following structure, with two basic interpretations based on whether a hard link can have a size or not.

Now, POSIX says that data blocks for a hard link “may be included” in pax archives, but the implications of this are not entirely clear. So the 512 bytes after the hard link are its data, and not the header of empty as we archived it? How can a hard link have different contents from its previous counterpart file?

This archive gives by far the richest and most surprising results I've encountered so far when extracting it with well-known tar utilities and libraries. The results below were produced using the latest releases of all packages at the time of writing.

This group is reasonable in principle: they ignore the size on the hard link, and extract file, its hard link cafÃ©, and empty.

This is the system tar utility of macOS, which is closer to POSIX in spirit regarding the concept of size on hard links, and writes the 512 bytes into the hard link. The end result is that file now contains the tar header of empty.

This group agrees with bsdtar that the 512 bytes are data of the hard link, but doesn't write them into the hard link. Instead, they skip forward over the data, and you are left with just file and cafÃ©, without empty.

This is where you begin to need more imagination. Because cafÃ© contains data, a separate file is created that contains the header of empty as data, while file keeps its original contents.

Makes cafÃ© a separate, empty file, and also extracts empty. Why not?

Does not extract cafÃ© at all, but to make up for it, it creates an empty directory PaxHeaders next to file and empty.

R has an entirely different approach: it extracts empty with 512 null bytes. It mistakenly applies the size to empty instead of the hard link, and those 512 bytes are from an end-of-archive marker.

Haskell's tar would be exactly like GNU tar, if only it did not have string decoding issues, which turn the file cafÃ© into cafÃÂ© on disk (in the year 2026, this is not a rendering quirk of your browser).

These implementations reject the tarball. I believe this is the best thing you can do, even if it's technically not POSIX-compliant.

This tarball is one of 134 tricky tarballs that I'm collecting and categorizing in my test suite haampie/tar-minefield, developed since the last post. Its website https://stoppels.ch/tar features a big table that shows how implementations deal with all these cases, as well as detailed info per test case. A variant from the tarball of this post is included as a test case.

If you'd like to discuss this, send me an email at firstname[at]lastname.ch.
