#9973. NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams: Bringing Real-Time Generative Simulation to Surgical Robotics

Surgical robotics is moving quickly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies. But evaluating and training these systems remains difficult. Physical robotic platforms are expensive to operate, experiments are slow to reproduce, and failures can damage instruments or biological material. Conventional simulators provide a safer alternative, but surgical scenes are exceptionally difficult to model: deformable tissue, fine instrument interactions, specular surfaces, sutures, needles, smoke, and occlusions all matter.

World foundation models offer a different path. Instead of manually authoring every object and physical interaction, they learn visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics. NVIDIA's Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator demonstrated this approach by generating future surgical video from an initial scene and a sequence of robot actions. It enabled faster-than-physical evaluation and synthetic data generation across the Open-H-Embodiment ecosystem.

Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics. Cosmos-H-Dreams distills the capabilities of Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator into a causal, few-step student model and serves it through FlashDreams, NVIDIA's accelerated streaming-inference library. Running on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the result is an interactive environment that a person or a learned policy can control in a closed loop.

Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator is an action-conditioned world foundation model built on NVIDIA Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B and post-trained on the Open-H-Embodiment dataset. Given a surgical context frame and a future robot trajectory, it generates video showing the likely visual consequences of those actions. This makes it useful for offline policy evaluation and synthetic data generation. A recorded or policy-generated trajectory can be sent to the model, the corresponding rollout can be generated, and the result can be inspected or scored without repeatedly executing the motion on a physical robot.

Cosmos-H-Dreams moves the model into the real-time regime. Starting from the multi-embodiment surgical priors learned by Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator, we specialize the model for da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) tabletop suturing and distill it into a causal student that generates the scene autoregressively. The released model receives an initial RGB frame and a live stream of robot kinematics, then produces the next chunk of frames before continuing with the following action block.

We have also demonstrated the versatility of Cosmos-H-Dreams by collaborating with CMR Surgical and Cambridge Consultants to integrate it with the Versius surgeon controller, enabling real-time operation on the Versius platform.

The key challenge is preserving useful surgical dynamics while reducing the cost of generation. Cosmos-H-Dreams uses a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long, autoregressive rollouts.

The bidirectional teacher begins from the Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator Open-H checkpoint, which uses a unified 44-dimensional action representation. For the released dVRK tabletop model, the dual-arm dVRK action content, consisting of relative end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper state, is mapped into this common representation.

The teacher is then fine-tuned on the JHU dVRK tabletop mixture, including successful demonstrations as well as failure and out-of-distribution episodes such as needle drops, missed throws, and unsuccessful knot ties. These failures are important: a simulator intended to evaluate policies must reproduce the consequences of poor actions, not only ideal demonstrations.

To improve stability during long rollouts, the training process progressively increases the teacher's temporal horizon. We start training on a 12-frame horizon and progressively increase this number until 72 frames. At each horizon bump, we initialize the warmed-up model with pretrained weights.

The teacher's denoising trajectories are first precomputed and cached. A causal student is initialized from the teacher and trained to imitate these cached trajectories. This warmup stage teaches the student to operate with causal attention and a streaming key/value cache before it begins learning from its own generated history.

Autoregressive models face a familiar problem: during training they may see clean, ground-truth context, while during deployment they must condition on their own imperfect outputs. Small errors can therefore compound over time.

Cosmos-H-Dreams addresses this mismatch with self-forcing distillation. During training, the student rolls forward using its own generated context. Distribution-matching supervision from the frozen teacher then guides those self-generated rollouts toward realistic surgical video. This prepares the student for the same conditions it will encounter during interactive inference.

The resulting model supports few-step diffusion, with as few as two denoising steps per latent frame, rather than the many-step process used by the full teacher. It combines the teacher's surgical priors with the causal structure needed for streaming.

Model distillation is only part of the real-time story. Cosmos-H-Dreams is served through FlashDreams, an accelerated inference library for autoregressive world and video models.

FlashDreams turns the distilled student into a low-latency streaming system through several complementary optimizations, such as streaming KV cache, CUDA Graph capturing, or model compilation.

Together, these techniques bring the distilled surgical world model fine-tune from the roughly ten-frames-per-second regime of standard Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator inference to interactive operation (~160 frames per second) on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000.

Cosmos-H-Dreams also provides the human-machine interfaces that turn generation into interaction. A browser client can send keyboard commands and receive generated frames over WebRTC. A Meta Quest client can map tracked controller motion into robot actions and display the synthesized scene through WebXR. The same model can also be connected to a learned surgical policy, with generated observations and predicted actions exchanged inside a closed loop.

While Cosmos-H-Dreams includes a pre-trained checkpoint for tabletop suturing, the system is designed to be extensible to your specific embodiment. To train a real-time student model for your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and self-forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide.

Cosmos-H-Dreams opens a new frontier for surgical simulation: environments learned from real robot data that are responsive enough to be inhabited.

The immediate next step is to evaluate more than visual quality. A useful surgical simulator must respond correctly to actions, preserve instrument and scene structure over long rollouts, and support conclusions that transfer to the physical robot. This motivates a new family of closed-loop benchmarks: tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action diversity, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and real policy outcomes.

Real-time world models can also become active partners in surgical policy development. They can generate rare failures on demand, provide scalable environments for reinforcement or imitation learning, and enable rapid evaluation of new policies without tying every experiment to scarce robotic hardware.

Further ahead, real-time simulation enables a series of downstream applications such as latency-aware telesurgery, where the world model helps maintain a more stable display; or interactive surgical rehearsal, procedure planning, and intraoperative decision support. Cosmos-H-Dreams is a research and development platform, not a diagnostic system, a replacement for intraoperative imaging, or a controller for a physical surgical robot. Yet it provides a foundation for exploring these possibilities safely.

As model fidelity, temporal stability, and hardware efficiency continue to improve, real-time generative simulation can help connect surgeon education, synthetic data generation, policy training, and policy evaluation within one shared Physical AI environment.

Explore the models, data, and runtime behind Cosmos-H-Dreams:

Cosmos-H-Dreams brings action-conditioned surgical world modeling into the real-time loop, creating a new environment for people and policies to practice, explore, generate data, and evaluate what happens next.

This is a fascinating leap for surgical robotics. Real-time generative simulation could greatly reduce risks in training and planning. The concept of distilling a large model into a causal student model is clever. If you're also exploring video generation from images, check out the Seedance 2.5 image-to-video tool for creative applications.

Assessing more than just visual quality is the immediate next step. A practical surgical simulator must enable findings that translate to the real robot, maintain instrument and scene organization during extended rollouts, and react appropriately to actions. Tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action variety, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and actual policy outcomes are some of the new closed-loop benchmarks that are motivated by this.

The progress in surgical robotics is genuinely exciting! 🏥🤖 Being able to train and test advanced vision-language-action systems in realistic simulations without risking expensive equipment or delicate procedures could make development much faster and safer. The level of detail needed for tissues, instruments, smoke, and lighting really shows how challenging this field is. 👏

It’s impressive to see technology moving beyond simple teleoperation and towards smarter, more capable robotic assistance. 🚀 Better simulation environments can help researchers refine these systems before they ever reach an operating room, which is a win for both surgeons and patients. 😊📱

Looking forward to seeing how projects like NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams shape the future of healthcare. 🌍💙 If these simulations continue becoming more realistic, they could play a huge role in improving surgical training, reducing costs, and ultimately delivering better patient outcomes. Amazing work and an exciting glimpse into what's ahead! 🙌✨

#9972. AMD winds up Zen 6 cores for faster clock speeds

Chips boast up to 256 cores, clocks up to 5.3 GHz, and IPC gains of 20 to 31 percent, just not all on the same SKU

After teasing its 256-core Epycs for more than a year, AMD is finally ready to talk about architectural changes to the Zen core that not only make it possible, but will eventually power its next generation of Ryzen processors in desktop and mobile PCs.

During a press event in Las Vegas last week, AMD spilled the beans on its latest Zen cores, which promise an average 27 percent uplift in instructions per clock (IPC) across a variety of AI and server workloads, along with boosted clocks ranging from 4.1 to 5.3 GHz. We expect to see even higher frequencies on consumer chips before long, but AMD isn’t quite ready to talk about Ryzen just yet.

CPU performance is a function of power, IPC, and clocks, and with gains across all three, the cores are shaping up to be one of the company’s biggest generational jumps ever.

As in past Epyc launches, Zen 6 isn’t one core. It comes in two flavors: a frequency-optimized variant (Zen 6) and a density-optimized version (Zen 6c).

This split dates back to the launch of AMD’s Bergamo Epycs in 2023, which packed 128 compact Zen 4c cores into just eight chiplets. The chip’s debut drew comparisons to Intel’s still relatively new Efficient (E-cores) for obvious reasons. But under the hood, AMD’s Zen 4c was nothing like what Intel was doing. The core itself was nearly identical to Zen 4; it simply traded clocks and a bit of cache per core for a more densely packed CPU die.

The only difference between running an application on Bergamo or Genoa was how quickly it executed. The same could not be said of Intel’s P and E cores, which used different ISAs.

This remained a defining characteristic and advantage of AMD’s compact core architecture through Zen 5, which allowed it to ship Turin parts with up to 192 cores without users having to worry about whether their app was running on a compact core or not.

With Zen 6c, at least as we understand it, this philosophy is largely unchanged. Both Zen 6 and Zen 6c share the same ISA, with clock being the main differentiator. There are other micro-architectural differences between the two cores designed to balance IPC and clock speeds more effectively.

Looking at the core’s block diagram, this isn’t immediately obvious. Zen 6 and Zen 5 share a very similar front and backend.

We'd be tempted to call the core iterative if it weren't for the 20 to 31 percent IPC uplift for cloud and AI workloads that AMD claims over Zen 5. This suggests that core for core, a 4.1 GHz Zen 6c-based Venice Epyc should deliver performance on par with a Zen 5-based Turin Epyc running at 5 GHz.

That's a pretty sizable jump, but just because AMD is seeing generational performance uplift in enterprise server and cloud workloads doesn't mean we'll see the same gains on the client side. Many will recall the roughly 5 percent performance gains gaming PC enthusiasts reported with the Ryzen 9000-series, leading to the rather unfortunate turn of phrase "Zen 5 percent."

That happened because game engines at the time simply weren't CPU-bottlenecked, and so faster cores could only raise the ceiling so much. Even so, AMD fellow and "Zen daddy" Mike Clark tells El Reg that PC buyers expect more than a 6 percent gain from Zen 6.

We're glossing over a bunch of low-level architectural optimizations here, but according to Clark, one of the biggest drivers of performance was the front end. Zen 5 introduced a dual front end, which for simple workloads worked great, but lost a lot of steam when confronted with more dynamic loads.

"The Zen 6 team did a really good job for those larger footprint workloads that have a bipolar nature," Clark said. "It's not something that comes through. You're not going to see it in a block diagram very well. It's sort of subtle... but it's a big lever."

Another contributor was the move to a distributed scheduler in the out-of-order pipeline. One of the biggest performance drivers in modern CPU cores is that they don't execute instructions in the order they receive them. Instead, they reorder the instructions so as to keep the core's backend execution units fed with a constant stream of instructions.

This is where we see the biggest difference between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. To account for the slower clocks on the latter core, AMD gave the core's scheduler deeper queues, which Clark tells us helps with higher-latency workloads. Meanwhile, from what we understand, Zen 6's shallower queue enables it to clock higher on less power.

Finally, on the backend, AMD made several subtle changes which should have major implications for vector heavy workloads, including AI. One of the more significant was the ability to perform four AVX2 or two AVX-512 loads per cycle.

While this doesn't improve AVX-512 performance much, for applications that haven't been updated to use it, the core is now able to perform twice as many loads, which should improve throughput for legacy applications. This should come in handy, particularly on PCs, where Intel's outright lack of AVX-512 support has made AVX2 the lowest common denominator for a lot of software.

That's not to say AVX-512 didn't get some love this generation. For those running AI workloads on CPUs, Zen 6 now natively supports FP16 datatypes. Previously FP16 was supported, but required padding the data to FP32, which meant the lower precision didn't buy much in terms of performance. That's no longer the case in Zen 6.

And while we're on the topic of AI acceleration, Clark notes that Zen 6 doubled the VNNI-INT8 pipes from two to four, and should effectively double throughput for workloads that support it.

While not strictly part of the core, AMD's Zen 6 processors also address one of the biggest asymmetries associated with its frequency and density optimized cores.

Going back to Bergamo, opting for a density-optimized Epyc didn't just come at the expense of clocks, but cache too. Each Zen 4c or Zen 5c chiplet contained twice as many cores, but the same amount of L3 cache.

16 channels of DDR5, 5 GHz clock speeds, and support for CXL 3.1 memory god boxes? What's not to like?

With Zen 6 and Zen 6c, you may be giving up some clocks, but cache per core is now a constant 4 MB. As we discussed in a Venice deep dive back in September, each of the processor's eight CPU dies contains 12 or 32 cores and 48 and 128 MB respectively.

The benefit here is that users don't have to worry about different ISAs or cache hierarchies when optimizing their software stacks against AMD's Epyc processors. The same cannot be said of Intel's Xeon processors.

As we alluded to earlier, Chipzilla's performance and efficiency cores use different micro-architectures, ISAs, cache hierarchies, clocks, and even cluster their cores differently. This can pose real headaches if you have workloads that take advantage of fat vector registers like AVX-512, or accelerators like AMX, which will work just fine on Intel's P-cores but won't even run on their E-cores.

This, along with support for SMT (Hyperthreading), which Intel has dropped for now, could help the House of Zen vacuum up even more market share from its long-time rival. ®

#9971. Andrew Kensler's permute(), a function for stateless, constant-time pseudorandom-order array iteration

That subtitle is a little bit of a mouthful, but I’ve been wanting to talk about Andrew Kensler’s permute() function for a while and I wanted to make it clear right off the bat why it’s useful. permute() is used some in the graphics community, especially in offline rendering, and the techniques are more widely known in cryptography*, but it’s applicable to so much more than graphics and cryptography.

Let’s first talk about the problem it solves. You want to iterate over \(k\) items of an array of length \(n\), in random order, where \(k \leq n\). Those \(k\) items cannot contain duplicates from the original array (they must each correspond to a unique index). Or, you want to get a random sample of \(k\) items without replacement.

When I say “random”, this is obviously pseudorandom, but there are varying degrees of pseudorandomness. This is unquestionably not cryptographically secure, that’s not its intended use. I can’t say that I know enough about pseudorandomness to say how statistically indistiguishable from random this is or for what applications it will be random enough. It’s good enough to use for computing rendering integrals, and I’d be comfortable using it for a lot of casual statistical analysis.

Update May 27, 2021: I saw what looks to be a nice improvement to the randomness of this, and extends it to work for 64-bit integers. I recommend taking a look after reading this post!

Anyway, the canonical way to randomly iterate over an array is to first shuffle it with the Fisher-Yates shuffle, and then iterate over the shuffled array.

*I found this Stack Overflow answer from 2009 that gives the exact same idea, so I should be clear that Andrew Kensler didn't really invent the method I'll talk about here, but I think he popularized the use of it in graphics and certainly created the particular hash function I'll show at the end.

uniform_rand_int(min, max) is inclusive of both min and max, i.e. \(\textnormal{swap\_idx} \in \{i, i+1, \dots, n-1\}\)

Obviously this manipulates the array in place, which may not be desirable for a bunch of reasons. In practice you might call this with an array of indices or an array of pointers.

There are a bunch of situations where the Fisher-Yates shuffle doesn’t work very well, because you need to store the shuffled array.

In the latter two cases there’s obviously a lot more to think about, like the cost of just reading incoherent values from the large array. There are other good ways to solve #2 and #3 too, especially if you’re doing distributed computing. But a lot of the techniques I know share the problem that you need to scan over the entire array at least once. If you have constant-time access into the array, Kensler’s method is always linear only in the size of your random sample, not in the original array.

In other words, if you want to iterate over \(k\) random, unique items from an array of length \(n\), then the Fisher-Yates shuffle is \(O(n)\) time and \(O(n)\) memory. As I’ll show in a second, this can be reduced to \(O(k)\) time and \(O(k)\) memory. But permute() is \(O(k)\) time and \(O(1)\) memory, the best you could possibly do. Not only that, but with permute() you can arbitrarily query random indices in constant time, which means you can use it in parallel across multiple threads or computers.

I think it’s worth mentioning you can extend the Fisher-Yates shuffle to handle #2. You use a sparse map to keep track of swapped indices rather than putting them into the array. When you swap the next index, you check your map to see if the original or swapped locations in the array have already been swapped. If so, you use the values from the map, otherwise you just use the original indices, and then you update the map. Here’s a code snippet to show what that looks like. This will select \(k\) random unique integers from the values \(\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}\).

But still, even this “incremental” Fisher-Yates shuffle requires \(O(k)\) memory, which makes it unsuitable for case #1 or case #3.

Update: I believe this is equivalent to, but less elegant than, Floyd's algorithm for random sampling without replacement. So if you want to use that (like if you're in case #2 and really care about good randomness), implement Floyd's algorithm, rather than the way I've framed it here.

Kensler introduced permute() in his paper Correlated Multi-Jittered Sampling. I didn’t quite understand how it worked when I first read it, so I also wanted to write this blog post to break it down and hopefully help others appreciate it. However if you just want the code, skip to the bottom!

The function acts as a “stateless” pseudorandom iterator over an array. It takes in a seed value for a permutation, the length of the array, and the index you’d like to map to a different index. It looks like this:

and if you wanted to use it, say to get 10 random unique values from a vector, you might do:

So how do we construct this magic function?

The first thing we need is a hash function that is invertible for a given power-of-two sized domain. What does that mean? For a given number of bits \(n\), every value from \(0\) to \(2^n-1\) will be hashed to a single unique value in the same range. It’s a one-to-one and onto mapping, i.e. a bijective function. Let’s give a super simple example: adding 1. Let’s say our domain is 2-bit integers. If we add one to a 2-bit number, we’ll get a unique 2-bit number.

Adding is generally, an invertible hashing operation. Another invertible operation in binary is multiplying by an odd number, let’s say 3. \(f(x) = (x * 3) \mod 4\), with:

A non-invertible operation is multiplying by two or any even number:

Kensler outlines more invertible operations in power-of-two domains, especially xor’s and combinations with a seed value, where different seed values give different permutations. Ultimately, we get some invertible hash function:

Already, we can see that this hash will allow us to randomly iterate over an array with length power-of-two. But what about arrays of other lengths? Kensler uses a technique from cryptography called “cycle walking”, which was invented in “Ciphers with Arbitrary Finite Domains” by Black and Rogaway. Cycle-walking is a fancy name, but the idea is simple: we just repeat the hash until the value is less than the length of the array! So we get a permute() function like this:

Obviously this can be really slow since it could take a lot of hashes to get to where we want, but we’ll get to that in a second. First, why does this work at all? This is where the bijective mapping comes in. We start with an index that is less than the length of the array and we hash it until we get another value less than the length of the array. Let’s visualize it like this:

where \(hash^3(x)\) is \(hash(hash(hash(x)))\) or, if you prefer the function composition notation, \(hash \circ hash \circ hash(x)\). In this case, I’ve bolded the first two hashes to indicate that the values are bigger than the length of the array. The last hash is our final permuted value.

Because our hash function is invertible, we can invert the final hashed value (note that we don’t need to actually implement the inverse, this is just theoretical):

By inverting the final value, which was less than the length of the array, we again get a value larger than or equal to the length of the array. So if we did this loop in reverse until we got a value less than the length of the array, we would get back the original index.

In other words, our loop is also an invertible hash function. But rather than mapping within a power-of-two sized domain, it maps within the domain of the array’s length, which is exactly what we’ve been trying to achieve.

We need to make this faster, specifically we don’t want a lot of loop iterations. Let’s say that we have a really good hash function such that there’s roughly a 50% probability that any bit (within our power-of-two domain) will be 1 after hashing. Now, we modify our hash function to specify the power-of-two domain. We do this by taking in a mask that limits the bits which get hashed. Here’s an example (but a bad hash function).

If our hash domain is the two-bit (unsigned) integers, then our mask would be 11 in binary, or 0x3. If our domain is the 32-bit integers, it would be 0xFFFFFFFF.

Now, in our permute() function, we’ll use a mask with all the bits set up to the most significant bit of the highest possible index (that is, len - 1). Here’s a really inefficient (\(O(\log n)\)) implementation for clarity:

However a lot of processors (e.g. x86 processors) have a single instruction that can get the number of leading zeros of an integer. In GCC you can use this with the instrisic __builtin_clz(x), which even on processors that don’t have the instruction will compile to a constant-time operation. So if you use GCC you could write:

This may not be super portable, here is how Kensler does it with bit arithmetic.

With this, our permute() function looks something like:

Because of this mask, we know that our hashing domain is less than two times the size of the array. Since our hash function has a 50/50 chance of flipping the most significant bit, or rather of hashing to a value in the lower half of its domain, we can say that on average, this will take less than two iterations. We’ve got our fast random iterator!

We still need to make a good invertible hash function. As I mentioned, Kensler outlines a bunch of invertible operations, and he uses hill-climbing to find a good hash function. I won’t go into that in more detail, but here is the final code using his hash. I’ve adapted Kensler’s code to the way I’ve structured this blog post:

Okay, there’s one additional thing at the end, the (static_cast(idx) + seed) % len, but that won’t break anything and adds a little extra randomness. The cast to 64-bit is necessary to prevent an overflow bug that could lead to repeats.

I hope that you find this as elegant and useful as I have! One final note: Kensler mentions that this hash only works well up to domains of about \(2^{27}\). For larger domains you could maybe use two calls of the permute function, although if it’s not random enough, that could exacerbate correlations. Overall I really just wanted to present the ideas here.

InfoQ Homepage News Java News Roundup: TornadoVM, A2A Java, Open Liberty, Open J Proxy, Gradle, EclipseStore

Nov 09, 2026 4 min read

This week's Java roundup for November 2nd, 2026, features news highlighting: point releases of TornadoVM, TornadoInsight, A2A for Java, Gradle and EclipseStore; the November 2026 edition of Open Liberty; the third release candidate of Open J Proxy; the second release candidates of Micrometer Metrics and Micrometer Tracing; and the third beta release of Quarkus 4.0.

Build 23 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 22 that include fixes for various issues. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

The release of TornadoVM 8.1.0 delivers bug fixes and notable changes such as: the ability for a TornadoVM kernel read and write a device allocation owned by another library owns, in place, without copying it and without writing a TornadoVM array header into it; and a change in the overloaded initializeDeviceAsync() method, defined in the TornadoExecutionPlan class, to initialise a device during application sets up. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Beehive Lab has also released version 2.1.0 of TornadoInsight, their IntelliJ IDEA plugin for TornadoVM. This release includes bug fixes, documentation improvements and new features such as: a new experimental AI-assisted transformation of a Java method into a TornadoVM kernel; and a new TornadoToolchain record that checks the TornadoVM SDK with the project JDK, builds the classpath, compiles with the project JDK, and creates a launcher. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of A2A Java SDK 1.5.0, a Java library that implements the Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A) for running agentic applications as A2AServers, ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a new OpenTelemetryPushNotificationSenderDecorator class to create a CLIENT enumeration, defined in the OpenTelemetry SpanKind enum class, to reflect the actual delivery outcome of success or failure; and the ability for authorized JPA task listings to offer optional provider capabilities so that supported policies can directly filter both the database count and page queries that for reduced scan and deserialization costs. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The third beta release of Quarkus 4.0.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: support for Valkey in the Quarkus Redis Client extension; and a new @CheckedTemplateParam annotation to support explicit naming of parameters in methods annotated with @CheckTemplate without the required -parameters compile flag. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The GA release of Open Liberty 26.0.0.11 delivers bug fixes, resolutions to numerous CVEs and new features such as: the ability to configure the timeout of the server quiesce stage, via the quiesceTimeout element, that was once fixed at 30 seconds; and improved validation that blocks form login error page redirects to external hosts unless the target host is listed in the wasReqURLRedirectDomainNames attribute of the element.

The third release candidate of Open J Proxy 1.1.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: support for PostgreSQL and MariaDB coverage in the C++ ODBC client; and a simplification of building and using the C++ ODBC drivers across all major OS platforms. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of Gradle 9.9.0 provides notable changes such as: the ability for Kotlin DSL scripts to be incrementally compiled using the Kotlin Build Tools API for improved build performance; new test filters that may be applied to JUnit Platform tests that are not declared as methods; and improvements to the Problems API that provides a predefined hierarchy of problem groups from the Problems interface. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of EclipseStore 4.3.0 delivers bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: A refactor of the VectorIndex interface, part of the JVector Index, to handle large indices and concurrent load and crash safety; and a new, lightweight VanillaJS storage viewer for the storage REST Interface that now deprecates the existing standalone Vaadin/Spring-based client GUI. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The second release candidate of Micrometer Metrics 1.18.0 ships with dependency upgrades and one new feature that adds support for fractional updates in Micrometer Atlas counters that had previously truncated them to a type long. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Similarly, the second release candidate of Micrometer Tracing 1.8.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: more efficient allocation of OpenTelemetry baggage reads by directly searching retained/current baggage and building the bulk results in one map; and an elimination of allocating wrappers while clearing an already empty context by reusing the NOOP function, defined in the CurrentTraceContext.Scope interface in conjunction with an instance of the Tracer.SpanInScope interface. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Andres Almiray, Java Champion and creator of JReleaser, has introduced his roadmap for JReleaser 2.0. Over the next several weeks, developers can expect changes that include:

A 2.0.0-SNAPSHOT release has been created and there will be numerous breaking changes.

#9969. GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

Aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

The reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

Six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

The same pattern shows up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

That shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

These deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

In the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that new capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

Maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

Intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

Provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every new request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

The discipline is new enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

How much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

This is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

Agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this issue.

Good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

Taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

That's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

#9968. Google Summer of Code 2026 results

The Rust Project participated in Google Summer of Code (GSoC) for the third time this year. This time we had 13 projects, and our dear contributors have been working very hard on them for several months. As usual, the projects had various durations, so while some of them have ended in August, the last one has only finished in November, so we have been waiting until we have all the results before publishing this blog post.

We are very happy to announce that all 13 projects were successful and passed their final evaluation! We consider it to be a testament to the diligence of our contributors, and the helpfulness of our mentors, that we are able to keep a very high rate[1] of successful GSoC projects several years in a row.

At the start of summer, we had a video call with our contributors, so that we could all get to know each other a bit, and learn about their projects. Over the following few months, we continuously communicated with the contributors, provided guidance and answered their questions and reviewed their pull requests. And most importantly, we learned many new things together! It was an overall great experience. We are grateful for all Rust contributions done by our GSoC participants and for the time we spent working together, and we hope that we will continue seeing at least some of them around in the future.

We would like to thank all our Rust GSoC 2026 contributors. You did a great job!

Even though this year we had fewer projects than in 2025, mostly due to limited mentoring capacity, Google Summer of Code 2026 was again a success for the Rust Project. We think that GSoC is a great way of introducing new contributors to our community, and we are looking forward to participating in GSoC (and other mentorship programs, such as Outreachy) again in the near future. If you are interested in becoming a (GSoC) contributor, check out our GSoC project idea list and our guide for new contributors.

Below you can find a brief summary of our GSoC 2026 projects. You can find more information about the original goals of the projects here. For easier navigation, here is an index of the project descriptions in alphabetical order:

And now strap in, as there is a ton of great content to read about here!

Marcelo worked on improving the usability of cross-vendor GPU programs in Rust using the std::offload module. At the start of the project, the offload prototype was only a proof of concept. It assumed that the offloaded code was bug-free, and it required users to write a lot of boilerplate code. Marcelo resolved both issues over the summer.

First, he implemented proper type checking. Marcelo extended the compiler to verify that the arguments passed to any offload call are of the correct type, as expected by the GPU kernel. Kernel launches are thus now safe.

After that, he added support for generic kernels. The compiler now collects all generic instantiations launched from the CPU side, and loads that info later when compiling GPU kernels to make sure we instantiate them as needed. Marcelo also added support to select which GPU to use, which is helpful for laptops with both an integrated and a dedicated GPU, as well as for servers with multiple GPUs. He also added two macros that removed the need for any boilerplate when writing and launching GPU kernels.

The hardest part of this project by far was dealing with references. Due to Rust semantics, we cannot just map types containing mutable references to GPUs and then process them using multiple threads. Previous Rust GPU projects used raw pointers as a workaround, but we obviously wanted to avoid those. Marcelo managed to implement a sound abstraction so that users can now safely declare how their kernels will access mutable arguments.

As a cherry on top, Marcelo also ported the RajaPerf performance suite from C++ to Rust and used it to benchmark his pull requests. His safe Rust version matches the performance of the original C++ code, and is now described in a GPU offload paper that he is working on together with his mentor, Manuel. This was Marcelo's second Rust GSoC project, and same as last year, we are very happy with the results. Great job!

The goal of this project was simple on paper: teach the Wild linker to link WebAssembly (Wasm) programs. However, adding support for a new linker target is of course far from simple. Luckily, Kei already had a lot of experience with Wild, as this was his second GSoC project working on the Wild linker.

And as expected, Kei did a great job! Prior to GSoC 2026, Wild had no Wasm output support. Now, the Wasm support is sufficiently good that Wild can link a range of complex programs to Wasm. For example, it is able to link itself, SQLite, ripgrep, CPython and even the SpiderMonkey JavaScript engine.

And the linking performance is excellent! When compared to wasm-ld, the de-facto standard Wasm linker, which is based on the LLD linker, Wild is 2-15x faster, and uses 2-5x less memory. You can find more benchmarks in his final report, where he also explains that achieving this performance took quite some work, because Wild's ELF linking performance did not immediately translate to being fast when linking Wasm.

Even after this GSoC project ended, Kei has continued improving Wild's Wasm support, as well as contributing to other parts of Wild. Thank you for bringing fast linking to a new set of use-cases, Kei! You are a valued member of the Wild team.

The goal of this project was to build the experimental std::autodiff module, which implements automatic differentiation of Rust code, and the std::offload module, which allows offloading Rust code to GPUs, in the CI of the Rust compiler.

Shota has already been contributing to this area in the months leading up to this year's GSoC, so he had no issues getting started. After valiantly fighting with our CI, he made both modules available in the official nightly compiler channel. Rust users can thus now simply install them with a single rustup command, rather than having to compile rustc from source! This is a huge benefit for gathering feedback on these features in the wild, as it makes it much easier to experiment with them.

Beyond making these projects available via rustup, he also worked on making it simpler to build projects that use std::offload. The original compilation pipeline was derived from Clang's support for GPU offload, so it involved calling clang helper binaries. That is clearly not optimal, so Shota worked on replacing it by directly calling the underlying LLVM APIs from rustc.

The last piece of his project was enabling testing in CI for both offload and autodiff, which already helped prevent multiple regressions. Right now, the GPU offload pipeline only tests the CPU setup side, but his work allowed us to talk to GPU hardware vendors, two of which already agreed to provide the Rust Project with GPU hardware so that in the future we can also run those tests on dedicated GPUs.

Overall, the project was a success. Shota had to show a lot of patience and endurance when working with various CMake quirks and CI challenges. We would like to extend a special thank you for that!

miri is a tool that can detect undefined behavior (UB) in unsafe Rust code. It used to have a prototype of an interactive debugger called priroda, but it became unmaintained some time ago. The goal of this project was to re-establish priroda, to make it easier to use miri interactively, debug how and why is UB introduced in Rust programs, and also help rustc developers analyse MIR, one of the intermediate representations of Rust programs.

Mohamed successfully reached both main goals of this project. He created a miri interface for the gdb debugger, which allows debugging programs executed by miri. You can set breakpoints, step through individual instructions, analyse MIR local variables and inspect the debugged program's state, with miri acting as a "virtual CPU". So when you encounter your next miri UB report, you can actually debug the program state that caused UB by running priroda! Mohamed also created a command-line interface for priroda, which is used to test it in miri's CI. This will ensure that it keeps working properly and will not bitrot again.

Mohamed also added basic support for the Debugger Adapter Protocol, which allows using priroda together with IDEs such as Visual Studio Code. Currently, connecting priroda to an IDE is a bit involved, so the next step would be to build a plugin for an IDE that would allow showing all the extra state that miri has, which gdb doesn't know how to interpret.

Debugging programs executed by miri is very exciting. Thank you for all your work!

The goal of this project was to implement two new language features that were accepted in RFC 3323:

Ryosuke had to familiarize himself with the compiler's codebase and do a lot of implementation work to get both features working. This included implementing parsing of the new syntax, recording its metadata in the compiler's Abstract Syntax Tree, implementing resolution of the restricted crate paths, and finally adding checks to enforce both restriction rules. This all amounted to around five thousand lines of Rust code!

Once the new features were implemented and available on nightly, Ryosuke wrote a Call for Testing blog post. It had to be very exciting to announce to the world that he implemented two new features from scratch, and people can now play with them on the nightly channel! After the blog post was published, users reported a few issues, which Ryosuke promptly fixed. He also contributed to rustdoc to improve how the impl and mut restrictions are rendered in the generated documentation pages.

Now that the features are available on nightly, feedback is being gathered on them, with the plan being to stabilize them in 2027. If you would like to provide feedback on the impl and mut restrictions, you can do so in this issue.

The goal of this project was clear, and Ryosuke achieved it completely. Awesome work!

The goal of this project, which was done in collaboration with the Rust Embedded Working Group, was to improve the API ergonomics and type safety of the serialport-rs crate.

The serialport project is a bit different from some other projects which participated in this year's Google Summer of Code. It is more on the side of "facility management" than rocket science. Its challenges are taming finicky operating system APIs and making good abstractions, rather than full-blown software engineering.

Tanmay led many fruitful discussions about potential design decisions, and did a lot of field research on how other crates that depend on serialport actually use its API, to figure out how to make the upcoming breaking API changes less disruptive and painful for them.

Tanmay also worked on sanding off some rough edges of the serialport API, such as replacing Boxed trait objects with enums, and making errors explicit in places where the legacy API used to panic. Some of the work still waits for integration. It is targeting the upcoming serialport 5.0 release.

Christian (Tanmay's mentor) found working alongside Tanmay very motivational, and he was able to catch up with a lot of other unrelated work in order to integrate Tanmay's changes. He noted that working with Tanmay was fun and productive, and that it was pure joy to see him grow from his first contribution in the bonding phase to seasoned contributions. Thank you, Tanmay!

This was my first Google Summer of Code as well. It was challenging, motivating, fun and definitely worth it. I would show up again.

libc is a foundational crate that is used by thousands of other crates across the Rust ecosystem. For the past several years, its maintainers have been attempting to publish a stable 1.0 release of the crate. Because this crate has to support interoperating with C on many compilation targets with weird quirks, this requires an enormous amount of work. We already had a GSoC project for moving libc towards 1.0 last year, and the goal of Adam's project was to make more progress in that direction.

And we can happily say that progress was indeed made! The original goal of Adam's project was to deprecate a number of constants that were difficult to maintain and cleanup inconsistencies in handling 32-bit/64-bit variants of file and time handling functions[2]. Adam was able to resolve that in a few weeks, and then he moved on to resolve a number of various issues blocking the 1.0 milestone.

Saying that Adam was productive would be… an understatement. We could follow his work in real-time, because he was posting daily GSoC reports for 116 days (!) in a row. The diligence and consistency with which he tackled so many complicated issues was an inspiration to us. In fact, sometimes the libc reviewers were not able to keep up!

You can find all Adam's libc pull requests here. You might notice that many of them have lots of comments, and even more discussions happened in GitHub issues and on Zulip. In addition to implementing the necessary code, making changes that affect interesting C platforms and architectures also required him to do a ton of research, and a lot of considerations of edge cases and possible backwards compatibility breakages. His work also took him on a whirlwind tour of diverse platforms; Adam's contributions spanned FreeBSD, NetBSD, Android, Hurd, NuttX, AIX, VxWorks, Fuchsia, L4Re and more.

Even though more work will still be required to get libc to 1.0, Adam's contributions made a significant dent in this effort. Thank you very much for all your work!

Linker scripts are arcane commands that can be used to instruct a linker to construct the final binary in a custom way. The Wild linker used to implement only basic linker script functionality, which Vishruth greatly expanded during his GSoC project.

Thanks to that, Wild can now successfully link Linux kernel modules, and it's even close to being able to link the Linux kernel itself! Vishruth's work involved greatly expanding expression evaluation support, location counters, program headers, etc. In addition to adding support for many missing bits of linker script support, Vishruth implemented support for partial linking (-r) as this is needed in order to link Linux kernel modules. You can find all the linker script features that he implemented here.

Adding all those peculiar features to Wild required performing many cross-cutting changes to its codebase, which Vishruth managed to do really well. And it was not at the cost of performance! Wild now manages to link Linux kernel modules such as btrfs or amdgpu 2-4x faster than the BFD (GNU ld) or LLD linkers[3]. You can find more benchmarks in his final report.

Vishruth has continued to contribute to Wild even after his GSoC project ended and has become a valued contributor to the project. Thank you very much for making Wild better, Vishruth!

rust-analyzer uses rowan for its syntax trees, a library for Concrete Syntax Trees. rowan has served us well over the years, but it has some downsides that cause major performance problems and also smaller convenience issues. In particular, memory fragmentation causes rust-analyzer to consume much more memory than it actually needs (in the order of redundant gigabytes).

We wanted to rewrite rowan to change that. The problem was that many parts in rust-analyzer touch syntax trees, and in particular assists (code actions) of which we have a lot. They also use mutable tree editing, a feature of rowan that can be convenient but was a major obstacle in rewriting it to be more efficient.

During his project, bit-aloo first migrated all rust-analyzer code from mutable tree editing to SyntaxEditor, a new abstraction that was created specifically to avoid mutation. After that, he removed mutable editing from rowan altogether.

The migration process is incremental and rowan is still inefficient in various aspects. However, we believe that the parts which required changes to large amounts of code are behind us, and we can complete the migration with more focused changes. bit-aloo is continuing to work on that even after his GSoC project ended. And he was also accepted as a member of the rust-analyzer team, so congratulations! We would like to thank him for his work, and hope to continue working with him to improve rust-analyzer for everyone.

The std::arch module of the Rust standard library contains various intrinsic functions that provide architecture and vendor-specific functionality. Their implementation lives in the stdarch repository, which is included as a Josh subtree in the main compiler repo (rust-lang/rust).

When someone changes the intrinsics in the main repo, breakages can silently creep in, because the main repo does not execute all the stdarch tests in its CI. That can cause friction when we synchronize the changes between the two repositories. Ideally, we would run all of stdarch's tests in the main repo to detect any issues as soon as possible.

And that is where Sumit came in! Over the course of his GSoC project, he examined the (very!) complex ways the intrinsics are tested in stdarch, and started porting them over to the main repo. But this was not a matter of copying over a few lines of YAML. The compiler repo uses its own build system (called bootstrap) and a CI workflow structure that is quite different from the stdarch repository. Sumit thus had to first understand what is each test suite doing, reimplement it as a part of bootstrap and finally integrate it into the compiler's CI workflows.

We run ~90 CI jobs across several hardware architectures, operating systems and OS versions. Getting all that to work while testing vendor-specific intrinsics required a lot of diligent work… and a lot of patience. It took five months for one of the test suites to finally succeed on the main repo's CI, and it required Sumit to completely refactor how the suite worked, for it to be more compatible with bootstrap. As another example, a different test suite that Sumit also got to work required running the tests in an Intel CPU emulator on CI.

Sumit ported most of the stdarch test suites to bootstrap, including intrinsics verification against reference C implementations, checks for automatically generated source code being up-to-date, and various unit tests for individual intrinsics and CPU feature detection logic. There is one remaining test suite to port, but the ported tests are already helping us find issues, which is great.

You can check Sumit's rust-lang PRs here; notice that he was also contributing to other parts of Rust in the meantime! Sumit's work will help us make LLVM upgrades and land intrinsics changes more easily. Thank you, Sumit!

The goal of this project was to get rid of a very scary place in the Rust compiler's test suite: a directory called tests/ui/issues. It contained thousands of test files based on historical Rust issues, dating back all the way to 2012. The problem with those tests was that they were named only with an issue number (e.g. issue-37291). When such a test would break, it was quite difficult to figure out what was it even supposed to test, because there was little context attached to it.

Even though we already had a GSoC project to tackle this problem last year, due to the sheer amount of uncategorized tests, there were still over four hundred tests left in this directory by the time zedddie started working on this project.

For each test in this directory, zedddie had to first understand what was the test doing and dig through its original GitHub issue and any other related issues and pull requests. Then they had to figure out what would be the best location to move the test under, search for any possible duplicates, come up with a descriptive name for the test (that tends to be very difficult!), and finally add a short description to the test that explains the context of why the test was added in the first place. Rinse and repeat, for hundreds of tests.

zedddie rolled up their sleeves, and categorized over 300 tests in 30 pull requests. Together with other contributors helping out over this summer, zedddie was finally able to remove the last batch of uncategorized tests at the start of August. As zedddie said in their final report: "What is left to do: nothing, tests/ui/issues is gone".

While this work might sound a bit bland, its positive effect on the maintainability of our test suite, and improving the lives of Rust compiler contributors, is considerable. It is also apparently a great way to learn about cool niche edge cases of Rust that most Rust developers might not know about! After migrating the remaining uncategorized UI tests, zedddie continued contributing to the next trait solver and const generics. Thank you very much for helping us finally get rid of tests/ui/issues, zedddie!

The Rust debugging experience leaves a lot to be desired. One reason why we struggled to improve it is that many of our debuginfo test suites did not even run in CI for the past few years, as they were difficult to maintain. When something changed in the type visualizers, the implementation details of a standard library type or in debugger internals, someone had to go through tens of tests and manually update them. This was not sustainable, so the test suite rotted.

Luckily for us, Anthony took that affront personally. Even before his GSoC project, he spent considerable effort on improving the quality of debug visualizers of various Rust standard library types, and gained an impressive amount of knowledge about debuggers.

During his GSoC project, he completely overhauled how our debuginfo test infrastructure works, both for LLDB and GDB. Thanks to his improvements, we can now easily "rebless" the reference output when something changes, which makes it much easier to keep our test suite up-to-date. The new tests also record much more information about the internal state of the debugger recorded during the test, which helps with diagnosing issues that cause type visualizers to stop working.

In addition to redesigning the test suite, Anthony also actually managed to re-enable the LLDB tests on both Windows and Linux in our CI again (after several years of being skipped there!). This will allow us to avoid debuginfo regressions and make it easier to improve the Rust debugging experience. Oh, and it goes without saying that while doing all that, he also made numerous improvements to Rust type visualizers. You can find his PRs here.

Anthony's amazing contributions and his deep expertise in debuggers led to him being invited to the Rust Compiler team, which was much deserved. What else can we add, other than: thank you for your awesome work!

The support for platform-specific directories (platformdirs) has been a long-standing feature request for rustup, to have more fine-grained filesystem directory choices. This project investigated how that issue could be resolved.

The real complexity of this feature request lies within a decade worth of different assumptions that previous iterations of rustup and cargo have made: it turns out that quite a lot of them are no longer true if we were to implement platformdirs support truly faithfully.

Guicheng first worked on cleaning up the interactions between rustup self uninstall and $CARGO_HOME/bin as a warmup. This issue itself is a very good demonstration of all that compatibility baggage: somehow $CARGO_HOME/bin has become the default binary directory for all things Rust, so rustup ended up installing itself and all its proxies into it. As a result, it has been super annoying to many that everything in $CARGO_HOME is gone with rustup self uninstall.

After that, he started the actual implementation of platformdirs support in rustup. This was no easy task! Not because the code itself was hard to write, but because it takes a lot of effort to figure out what should be the desired behavior in the first place. Also, in order to determine the appropriate platformdirs semantics, some prior research is often required to see how things became what they are today, so the decoupling of different concerns could proceed, and migration paths could be designed accordingly. It was in this sense that this is different from a typical GSoC project, and luckily thanks to the effort he has put into this project, we have not only come up with the final patch, but also discovered and fixed some tiny preexisting issues with this long-untouched aspect of the rustup codebase along the way.

Thank you for digging into this complex topic, Guicheng!

We would like to thank all contributors who have participated in Google Summer of Code 2026 with us! Your contributions helped make Rust better, and introduced you as new members of our community, which is a reason to celebrate. We are looking forward to participating in GSoC again next year!

We would also like to thank Google for organizing the Google Summer of Code program and for allowing us to host a large number of projects every year. And last, but not least, we would like to thank all the Rust mentors who were tirelessly helping our contributors to complete their projects. Without you, Rust GSoC would not be possible.

#9967. Mozilla Thunderbird email service edges closer to launch with early access

Some waitlist members get a first look at Thundermail, a paid alternative to Gmail

The Mozilla-backed Thunderbird project is getting closer to a wider launch of a hosted email service designed to complement its desktop mail app.

Now known as Thundermail (what else?), the service was originally developed under the Thunderbird Pro banner, which encompassed paid email, appointment scheduling, and file-sharing services designed to generate additional revenue for the organization.

The org has been inviting people from its Thundermail waitlist to try the service through an early-access program, and this writer just happened to be among them.

Thundermail offers a web-based email interface and can also be accessed through the Thunderbird desktop app, the Thunderbird mobile app for Android, or other compatible email clients. The Thunderbird apps remain free.

Users get an inbox with up to 15 email addresses and three custom domains, plus 30 GB of mail storage and 60 GB of send storage for Thunderbird Send, an end-to-end encrypted file-sharing and large-attachment service. That’s for starters – the org intends to offer those extra features and services at different price points.

Yes, Thundermail is a paid service, which may put off some users who are used to free email accounts offered via Gmail, Outlook.com and Proton Mail, but with the first two of those you do get served ads along with your messages.

The sign-up screens for Thundermail suggest the basic service will cost $6 per month, billed annually. This is roughly equivalent to the £55 we paid for a year on the early access program.

We asked Thunderbird when we can expect to see Thundermail officially launched and open to all comers. We will update if we get an answer. It previously said that a full launch is expected sometime in 2026.

The web-based user interface of Thundermail presents a fairly clean and uncluttered look, and could be likened to Gmail with the screen partitioned into a pane with folders on the left and a larger one to the right displaying messages.

A welcome screen introduces you to the features of Thundermail, which include the ability to work on several drafts at once, schedule delivery times for emails, create folders to arrange messages, contact lists and identities – all pretty much standard for an email system.

We haven’t really had the time to test out Thundermail a great deal since signing up, but there are no great surprises so far, and everything works pretty much the way you would expect it to.

Firefox and the Thunderbird mail client both recently moved to a fortnightly release schedule in line with Mozilla’s plans, and Thunderbird itself gained support for Microsoft’s Exchange late last year. ®

We're thrilled to share that Baseten is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub!

Baseten joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub's model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

Baseten is an AI infrastructure platform that covers serverless AI, training and more. With a catalog of many frontier models, Baseten makes it easy for developers to integrate a wide range of AI capabilities into their applications with minimal setup.

Baseten supports a broad spectrum of model types - from LLMs to text-to-speech and more. As part of this initial integration, Baseten is launching support for conversational and text-generation tasks on Hugging Face, enabling access to popular open-weight LLMs such as Kimi K3, latest DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM-5.2, and many more. Support for additional tasks will roll out soon!

See the full list of models supported by Baseten here.

Follow Baseten on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/baseten.

Baseten is available through the Hugging Face SDKs - huggingface_hub (>= 1.26.1) for Python and @huggingface/inference for JavaScript.

The following examples show how to use the latest DeepSeek V4 Flash through Baseten. Use a Hugging Face token to authenticate - the request will be routed to Baseten automatically.

Hugging Face Inference Providers are integrated in most Agent Harnesses - including Pi, OpenCode, Hermes Agents, OpenClaw, and more. This means you can plug baseten-hosted models straight into your favorite tools without any extra glue code. Browse the full list of integrations here.

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a baseten API key you're billed on your baseten account.
